#9735. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9734. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9733. The Struggle to Secure Hardware Samples for Honest Tech Reviews

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

I’ve reached out to hardware vendors, including NVIDIA and AMD, seeking review samples for Tech Business News, but so far, all I’ve heard back is crickets.

Meanwhile, I watch channels such as Gamers Nexus and Linus Tech Tips, featuring Linus Sebastian, publishing hardware reviews while I’m still trying to arrange product access.

They’ve built substantial audiences, and I understand why manufacturers would see value in having their products reviewed by people with that kind of reach and recognition.

But I keep coming back to the same question: where does that leave smaller publications and individual reviewers who have experience and something worthwhile to contribute?

I founded Tech Business News in 2020 after spending roughly two decades working in IT, and I want to bring that practical background into hardware reviews.

The challenge has been getting equipment into my hands so I can form an opinion based on using it, then explain that experience honestly to readers.

When I watch established reviewers working through the latest hardware, access appears considerably easier from the outside than it has been through my own vendor enquiries.

I don’t know what arrangements sit behind each review, how equipment was obtained or how much work went into establishing those relationships with the companies involved.

What I do know is that I’ve approached vendors about reviewing their hardware and haven’t received the replies needed to move those conversations towards actual testing.

That’s frustrating when you’re trying to build coverage, particularly when the request is about obtaining access to equipment so you can assess it properly for readers.

A smaller audience doesn’t automatically mean a reviewer has less useful experience, just as a large audience doesn’t automatically establish the quality of an individual review.

There should be room for different perspectives, including someone who wants to explain what a product feels like to use outside a tightly controlled benchmark session.

My own interest in hardware starts with a fairly ordinary question: will someone notice a meaningful improvement after spending their money and installing the new component?

A CPU might have a slightly higher clock speed, but that alone doesn’t tell me whether my everyday experience will improve enough to justify an upgrade.

I want to know whether a game feels smoother, whether an application responds faster and whether the improvement remains noticeable once the excitement of upgrading wears off.

For me, chasing small benchmark differences can become a hobby in itself, especially when the discussion centres on advantages that are difficult to perceive during use.

There’s an audience for that level of comparison, but my preference is to investigate what those results translate into when someone sits down at their computer.

If I need a chart to distinguish between two experiences that otherwise feel much the same, I’d want to make that clear in my review too.

That doesn’t make the measured difference irrelevant, because some buyers have workloads where relatively small gains become useful, particularly when repeated across long periods of work.

It does mean I’d want to explain who benefits, under what circumstances, and whether someone using the hardware differently should expect to notice the same advantage.

With gaming hardware, I’m interested in the experience of playing, including whether movement feels consistent and whether interruptions become distracting during the parts that demand responsiveness.

An average frame rate gives useful information, but I’d also want to investigate stuttering and performance drops that might explain why a game sometimes feels uncomfortable.

Measurements can help identify those problems, while time spent playing helps me describe how they affect the experience and whether they would influence my buying decision.

My approach would combine those observations with enough testing detail for readers to understand what I experienced, including the settings and other hardware in the system.

I’m comfortable giving a personal opinion, provided I explain what supports it and acknowledge that someone with different equipment or priorities might reach a different conclusion.

That’s the kind of review I want to publish: a practical account of whether the hardware improved my experience and who might find that improvement worthwhile.

My years working in IT give me a foundation for assessing hardware, but they can’t replace direct access to the particular product I’m supposed to review.

I can read specifications and report a manufacturer’s claims, although an independent assessment requires testing that gives me something of my own to say about performance.

Without the product, I can’t investigate whether a promising specification becomes a useful improvement, or whether an unexpected limitation changes how I’d assess its overall value.

Buying hardware provides another route, but every purchase adds an expense before accounting for the time involved in preparing tests, investigating problems and writing the review.

For a smaller publication, those costs influence which products can realistically receive coverage and how often there’s an opportunity to compare equipment under similar testing conditions.

A loan sample could help make that work possible, with clear arrangements about testing timeframes and returns, alongside the editorial freedom needed to publish the findings.

I’m not suggesting that NVIDIA or AMD owes me equipment, and I can’t explain why my approaches haven’t received replies or assume what caused that silence.

I’d still appreciate an answer, even if it simply explained that review samples weren’t available, because that would give me something definite to work with instead.

At present, the silence leaves me trying to develop hardware coverage without knowing whether there’s a suitable contact or a realistic opportunity to arrange product access.

I want the chance to assess equipment through my own experience, bringing a smaller publication’s perspective to a conversation that already includes some very prominent voices.

If an upgrade makes a noticeable difference, I want to explain where I experienced it, while being equally clear when the benefit is harder to recognise.

Readers deciding whether to replace a working computer deserve that context, particularly when a technically faster component might deliver less practical improvement than they were expecting.

#9732. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9730. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 21st of October 2026 11:26 AM

i discovered this blog two months back from the idscan/Nexus story and was immediately impressed by the journalism on here. as soon as i heard about this doing the rounds elsewhere on social media my first instinct was “i wonder if krebs has written about it yet?” and lo and behold. well anyways, great work as usual, cheers

Maybe I should have kept my blog as pure HTML, perhaps with some perl, instead of going to WordPress.

Just don’t forget the cgi-perl and imagemaps.

Hugo, yes! I finally retired my old Drupal-based site last week and switched to Hugo. For my blog-like site, it’s perfect and saves cost, since it’s served as a static site.

This PHP flaw is a stark reminder of how much of the web runs on shared infrastructure — one critical bug can take government and business sites offline at once. I have been following the patching updates closely, and TrendWire has been a useful source for keeping up with the fast-moving security news around this story. Hopefully hosts patch quickly before mass exploitation ramps up, as the researchers warn.

#9728. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9725. When Blockchain Data Becomes AI Context, Stale State Becomes a Security Risk

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.

Why autonomous agents need more than accurate retrieval when interacting with wallets, smart contracts, and decentralised protocols?

Blockchain systems are designed to maintain a shared record of transactions and state changes. AI agents are designed to interpret information, reason about goals, and decide what to do next. On paper, combining the two looks straightforward: give an agent access to blockchain data, let it understand the current situation, and allow it to act.

But there is a problem hidden inside that workflow. The data an AI agent retrieves can be correct when it is fetched, but still be unsafe to use when the agent acts on it.

A wallet balance may have changed. A transaction that appeared pending may have been confirmed. A decentralised exchange pool may have lost liquidity. A lending position may have moved closer to liquidation. An indexed view of a protocol may not yet reflect the latest block.

None of these situations necessarily requires a model to hallucinate. The agent can interpret every field correctly, follow its instructions, and produce a perfectly reasonable plan based on information that no longer describes the system it is about to interact with.

That is the kind of failure I find particularly important when thinking about production AI systems. We often concentrate on model quality, retrieval accuracy, and the amount of context an agent can process. Those things matter, but they do not answer a more fundamental question: Is the context still valid when the system uses it?

This becomes especially important in blockchain applications because an AI agent may move from reading information to initiating transactions. A stale answer in a chatbot can be corrected. A stale decision that results in a confirmed financial transaction may be much harder to recover from.

The challenge, then, is not simply to give AI agents more blockchain data. It is to design a system that understands where that data came from, which version of reality it represents, and whether it remains trustworthy enough to support the next action.

Consider a hypothetical AI agent responsible for monitoring a decentralised finance portfolio. The agent retrieves a wallet balance, checks a lending protocol, compares liquidity across two decentralised exchanges, and recommends moving a portion of the portfolio to a different position. Its calculations are correct. The relevant contract addresses are correct. The transaction it prepares respects the configured spending limit.

Yet the decision is still unsafe. Why? Because the information used to construct the transaction came from different moments in time.

The wallet balance was retrieved several seconds earlier. The exchange liquidity came from an indexer that was still processing recent events. The lending position was read from a separate RPC endpoint. Meanwhile, another transaction changed the wallet's balance, and the market moved.

Each response may have been valid when generated. Together, they no longer represent a consistent view of the system. This is a familiar category of distributed-systems problem: different components observe changes at different times. Blockchain infrastructure makes the problem particularly visible because applications often combine on-chain reads, event streams, indexed datasets, external price feeds, and local caches. An AI agent adds another stage to this process. It does not necessarily execute an action immediately after retrieving information. It may reason through several alternatives, call additional tools, summarise results, or ask another agent for an assessment. By the time the plan is ready, its original observations may already be outdated.

The important distinction is between data correctness at retrieval time and decision validity at execution time. These are not the same guarantee. A blockchain node can return the correct balance for the state it queried. An indexer can correctly process every event it has received. A retrieval system can return exactly the record requested. None of those facts guarantees that the complete context remains suitable for a transaction several seconds later. This is why I believe context engineering becomes much more than a retrieval problem when AI agents begin interacting with financial infrastructure. Context must be treated as a representation of system state, with explicit limits on how long that representation can be trusted.

One reason stale context is difficult to manage is that blockchain applications rarely obtain all their information from a single source.

These mechanisms serve different purposes. For example, Ethereum's JSON-RPC documentation distinguishes methods used to inspect state from methods used to retrieve historical information and track network activity. An application that combines these responses must understand what each response represents rather than treating every result as an interchangeable snapshot of reality.

Indexing adds another consideration. Services such as The Graph process blockchain events and expose structured data that applications can query more conveniently. This removes much of the burden of reconstructing useful application state from low-level blockchain data. However, an indexed representation is still a processed view of the chain. It depends on the progress of indexing, the logic used to interpret events, and the consistency of the underlying data pipeline.

A query returning successfully does not, by itself, establish that the indexer has caught up with the block relevant to the agent's decision. There is nothing inherently wrong with these architectures. Indexed data is valuable, RPC access is essential, and event-driven systems are often more efficient than repeatedly polling every contract.

The mistake is allowing the agent to interpret successful retrieval as proof of freshness. A context pipeline needs to communicate not just what a value is, but also where it came from, what state it describes, and what the application can safely infer from it.

The first response to stale context is often to add a timestamp or configure a time-to-live, commonly called a TTL. That is a useful starting point, but blockchain applications need a more careful approach.

Imagine an agent retrieves a token balance at 10:00:00 and prepares a transaction at 10:00:03. Three seconds may be perfectly acceptable for a low-risk monitoring task. The same delay may be unacceptable for an operation that depends on a rapidly changing exchange price or a lending position near a liquidation threshold. Now consider the opposite situation. An indexed record was produced a minute ago, but it represents a fully finalised block, and the application only needs historical reporting. That record may be entirely suitable for its purpose.

Age alone does not determine whether information is safe to use. Freshness depends on the decision, the source, the rate at which the relevant state can change, and the consequences of acting on an incorrect assumption. For blockchain-aware agents, I would distinguish at least four dimensions.

Temporal freshness: How much time has elapsed since the observation was made?

Chain freshness: Which block does the observation represent, and how does that block relate to the network's current state?

Source freshness: Has the relevant RPC endpoint or indexer processed the changes needed for this decision?

Decision freshness: Have the assumptions that justified the proposed action remained valid throughout planning and execution?

The fourth dimension is particularly important. An agent can retrieve fresh data, spend time reasoning about it, and then act on a plan whose assumptions have become invalid. A simple TTL cannot fully solve that problem. A more useful design assigns freshness requirements to the type of action. Reading historical transfers for a portfolio summary may require a different standard from submitting a swap or changing collateral in a lending protocol.

The system should be able to say not only, "This observation is three seconds old," but also, "This observation satisfies the requirements for this decision," or, "This information must be refreshed before execution." That is a much stronger foundation for reliable autonomy.

Blockchain applications have an additional advantage when managing freshness: they can associate observations with chain-specific identifiers.

On an Ethereum-compatible network, an application can record the block number and block hash associated with a state observation. This provides more useful information than a wall-clock timestamp alone. Suppose an agent reads a lending position and records that the observation came from block 24,000,100. It then retrieves market data and a wallet balance. If those observations refer to different blocks, the system knows that they may not represent the same chain state. That does not automatically make the observations unusable. Different block references may be perfectly acceptable for monitoring or exploratory analysis. But if the proposed action depends on a consistent set of values, the mismatch should be visible to the system. Block identifiers also matter because blockchain history is not always immediately final. Depending on the network and the observation being used, a block that was initially considered the head of the chain may later be replaced during a reorganisation.

Ethereum's JSON-RPC interface exposes block tags, including latest, safe, and finalized. These represent different positions in the chain's progression and offer ways to express what kind of state they need. The appropriate choice depends on the operation.

A monitoring agent may benefit from observing the latest available state to detect an emerging opportunity. A system recording a final accounting result may require a stronger finality guarantee. An agent preparing a transaction should understand which assumptions depend on provisional observations and which must hold before execution. There is no universal rule that every AI agent should wait for finalized state before doing anything. Waiting may introduce unnecessary latency for some applications. The engineering task is to make the trade-off explicit.

The system should know whether it is making a tentative observation, a decision based on a sufficiently stable state, or a conclusion that requires finalised data. Without that distinction, a model may treat every retrieved value as equally authoritative, even when the underlying blockchain guarantees are different.

Stale data is only part of the problem. An agent can also receive individually accurate observations that do not belong together. Consider a lending application. One tool returns the latest collateral value. Another returns a debt balance from an earlier block. A third retrieves a health factor calculated by an indexer that has not yet incorporated a recent repayment.

The model sees three plausible values and constructs a coherent explanation. But the explanation is based on a mixed snapshot. This is similar to a database transaction that reads different versions of related records without a suitable consistency strategy. Each record may be valid on its own, yet the combined view may never have existed as a single coherent state.

For an autonomous agent, that inconsistency can become an action. It might conclude that a position is safe when it is not. It might recommend a repayment amount that no longer matches the outstanding debt. It might prepare a transaction that exceeds the available balance after another operation has completed.

The solution is not necessarily to force every read through one expensive data source. Instead, the architecture should define which values must be consistent for a particular decision. For a transaction that depends on multiple pieces of contract state, the system might query the relevant values at a common block reference where supported. It might reject a plan if observations are too far apart, refresh the relevant contract state, or simulate the transaction against a sufficiently current state before submission. If a source cannot provide the required consistency guarantee, the agent should know that limitation.

This is an important principle for context engineering: relevance determines which information the agent needs; consistency determines whether that information can safely be used together. A context window can contain all the right facts and still describe a world that does not exist.

This problem becomes more interesting when an AI agent maintains memory across multiple steps or sessions. Memory is useful because an agent should not have to rediscover everything whenever a workflow resumes. It may need to remember that a user prefers a particular protocol, that a transaction failed previously, that an operation requires additional approval, or that a previous analysis identified a potential risk.

But not every fact deserves to remain authoritative indefinitely. Suppose an agent records the following observation: The wallet has sufficient USDC to execute the planned transaction.

That statement may have been correct when the agent recorded it. Later, another process transfers some of the funds. If the original statement remains in memory and is retrieved because it is semantically relevant, the agent may treat an outdated observation as a current balance. The retrieval system has not necessarily failed. It found exactly the information that matched the question. The problem is that the information's validity changed after it was stored.

This is one reason I distinguish between memory and state. Memory can preserve what the system observed, what it previously decided, why it made that decision, and what happened afterwards. An authoritative state must come from the appropriate source at the time the system needs to use it.

For blockchain applications, that distinction can be represented explicitly. A memory entry might say:

The last point is essential. A stored transaction identifier is useful evidence for finding an operation. There is no proof that the operation succeeded. The same rule applies to protocol eligibility, contract permissions, exchange liquidity, and previously approved transaction routes. A historical approval should not automatically become permanent authorisation for future transactions.

This does not mean an agent should discard its memory frequently. It means memory should preserve the distinction between historical facts, current observations, and assumptions that need revalidation. In practical terms, every piece of context that can become invalid should have a clear validity model. Some information may be valid until a policy changes. Other information may need to be refreshed before every financial action. Still, other information is historical and should never be presented as the current state.

The goal is not to make agents forget more. It is to prevent them from confusing what happened with what is happening now.

There is a further complication that is easy to overlook: even if every observation was fresh when retrieved, the plan built from those observations can become stale while the agent reasons. Imagine an agent evaluating three possible transaction routes. It gathers pool liquidity, estimates gas costs, calculates expected output, and compares the results. It then selects a route and prepares a transaction.

Between selection and submission, a relevant market condition changes. The agent may still have the original context in its prompt. Its reasoning may remain internally consistent. But the decision made is no longer supported by the same conditions.

I think this is where the design of agent runtimes becomes especially important. Context freshness cannot be handled only when information enters the model. It must also be considered at the boundary between planning and execution. A useful approach is to associate a decision with the observations and assumptions that justified it. For example, a proposed transaction could record:

The system can then determine whether the proposal remains valid before it is signed. This is more reliable than asking the model, "Are you still confident in this transaction?" Confidence is not a substitute for checking whether the relevant state has changed.

If a critical assumption no longer holds, the proposal should be invalidated. The agent can retrieve fresh data, recalculate the plan, and request another authorisation if required.

That makes the decision itself a managed object with a lifecycle, rather than a paragraph in the model's conversation history. It also helps separate two responsibilities that should not be confused: the model proposes an action, while the runtime determines whether the proposal is still valid for execution.

If I were designing a reference architecture for a blockchain-connected AI agent, I would avoid treating context as a single object assembled at the beginning of a workflow and passed unchanged through every subsequent step.

Instead, I would introduce a context validation layer between data retrieval, decision-making, and execution. The workflow would look something like this:

flowchart TDA["Blockchain RPC, Events, Indexers, Oracles"] --> B["Data Normalization and Provenance"]B --> C["Context Validation"]C -->|Valid for decision| D["AI Agent: Reason and Plan"]C -->|Stale or inconsistent| E["Refresh or Reject"]E --> BD --> F["Transaction Proposal"]F --> G["Execution-Time Validation"]G -->|Conditions satisfied| H["Policy Engine and Secure Signer"]G -->|Assumptions invalid| EH --> I["Blockchain Submission"]I --> J["Receipt and State Verification"]J --> K["Update Workflow State and Memory"]K --> C

The architecture does not require the model to understand every detail of blockchain consistency. It requires the surrounding system to expose enough metadata and enforce the appropriate rules. The data normalisation layer identifies the source and meaning of each observation. The context validation layer evaluates freshness and consistency according to the intended task. The agent uses validated information to propose a plan. The execution-time validator checks the assumptions that matter before a transaction can proceed.

Finally, the monitoring layer verifies what actually happened and updates the workflow state. This last step matters because a transaction being accepted by an RPC endpoint is not the same as a transaction being confirmed on-chain. A transaction receipt, its execution status, and the resulting state changes provide different evidence about the outcome.

If the submission response is lost or a timeout occurs, the system must not immediately assume failure and blindly submit the same operation again. It should inspect the known transaction identifier, check the relevant transaction state, and determine whether the original operation is pending, confirmed, replaced, or otherwise unresolved. Only then should it decide how to continue. This is where context engineering and distributed-systems engineering meet. The model needs useful context, but the runtime also needs a reliable record of what has been observed, what has been proposed, what has been authorised, and what has actually happened.

A practical system cannot refresh every value before every operation. That would increase latency, consume infrastructure capacity, and potentially make an otherwise useful agent too expensive to operate. The better approach is to align freshness requirements with the risk of the action. Consider three different tasks.

A portfolio reporting agent might summarise historical transfers and estimate the distribution of assets across wallets. It can often work with indexed data, provided that the report identifies the relevant block or time range and makes its limitations clear.

A monitoring agent might watch a lending position and notify the user when its health factor approaches a configured threshold. It needs sufficiently current information to make the alert useful, but it does not necessarily need permission to submit a transaction.

An autonomous transaction agent might adjust collateral or execute a swap. Its decision depends on the current state of relevant contracts, applicable permissions, and transaction-specific constraints. It needs stronger validation immediately before execution.

These tasks can use similar data sources while requiring different levels of assurance. This suggests that context freshness should be part of the application's policy model rather than a universal setting. The system might define a maximum observation age for a specific task, require a particular block reference, or demand that critical values be re-read immediately before signing. It could also specify when a task must stop and request human intervention.

The precise rules will differ across chains, protocols, and applications. The important thing is that they should be explicit, testable, and enforced outside the model. A useful operational principle is simple: the higher the impact of an incorrect action, the stronger the evidence required before that action is allowed.

Testing this problem requires more than checking whether an agent answers questions correctly. A system may perform well on static test data because the same balance, contract state, and market conditions remain unchanged throughout each test. Production environments are different. State changes while the agent is reasoning, external services become temporarily unavailable, and observations arrive in an unexpected order.

I would test the complete decision lifecycle, including the conditions under which the system refuses to act. For example, consider a test suite with the following scenarios.

Refresh the balance and recalculate the transaction

Detect the indexing lag or use an appropriate alternative source

Observations refer to incompatible block states

Reject or reconcile the context before a state-dependent decision

Invalidate affected observations and re-evaluate the decision

Resolve the transaction's status before retrying

Transaction simulation no longer matches current conditions

Stored memory contains an outdated approval

Revalidate the current policy and authorisation

The external data source becomes unavailable

Fail safely rather than silently treating old information as current

These tests should run under controlled conditions where the team can reproduce the same failure and inspect the system's behaviour. I would also measure more than task completion. Useful metrics include the age of critical observations when an action is authorised, the frequency of decisions rejected for stale state, the proportion of indexed observations that lag beyond their allowed threshold, and the number of transaction retries that occur without a verified execution status.

Another useful measure is the stale-action escape rate: how often an action based on an invalid or inconsistent state reaches the execution boundary instead of being rejected. For high-impact operations, the target should be zero unauthorised executions caused by known freshness violations. Achieving that requires testing the controls around the model, not merely improving its ability to recognise outdated information in a prompt.

There is also a cost to consider. Refreshing every observation, querying multiple providers, and repeatedly simulating transactions can increase latency and infrastructure consumption. The engineering objective is to establish the minimum evidence required for each action without adding unnecessary checks to low-risk tasks. A good evaluation should therefore measure both safety and operational efficiency.

When an AI agent makes an incorrect decision, a log entry saying that a tool call succeeded is rarely enough to diagnose the failure. Suppose an agent executes a transaction based on a balance that had changed several seconds earlier. The transaction succeeds technically, but the resulting position violates the user's intended allocation.

To understand what happened, the team needs to reconstruct the decision. Which balance did the agent observe? Which block did it refer to? What did the indexer report? How old was the price data? Which assumptions did the plan depend on? Was the transaction simulated? Did the policy engine validate the proposal against the fresh state? What did the blockchain ultimately confirm?

Without this information, engineers may blame the model when the real failure occurred in the data pipeline or execution layer. I would treat decision observability as a first-class part of the architecture. For every consequential action, the system should maintain a trace linking the observations used, their provenance, the proposed transaction, the applicable policy checks, the authorisation result, and the confirmed outcome.

Sensitive information, particularly private keys and credentials, must never be exposed in these records. The objective is to preserve enough structured evidence to reconstruct the decision without creating another security vulnerability. This is also where context versioning becomes valuable. If a team can establish exactly which observations and policy versions supported a decision, it can reproduce the relevant conditions in a test environment and determine which safeguard failed.

Observability should answer a more useful question than "Did the agent call the tool?" It should answer: "Was the action justified by the information available, and did that information remain valid when the system authorised execution?"

One of the appealing properties of blockchain is that transaction history can be independently verified. But that property can create a misleading sense of security when applications consume blockchain information through multiple layers of infrastructure.

A verifiable ledger does not automatically make every API response current. A correctly indexed event does not guarantee that an application has processed every subsequent event. A valid price-feed response does not establish that its value is appropriate for every financial decision. Trust must be considered across the complete path from the underlying state to the action taken by the agent. That means understanding the guarantees offered by each component, monitoring where those guarantees can weaken, and refusing to let a successful response stand in for a stronger guarantee that the source never provided. The same principle applies to AI memory. A model may recall an observation accurately without knowing that the observation has expired. A retrieval system may rank an outdated record highly because it is relevant to the current query. A reasoning model may then produce a convincing plan that is no longer safe to execute. The answer is not to ask the model to be more careful. It is to give the surrounding system the information and authority needed to enforce the distinction between historical knowledge and the current state.

As AI agents move toward financial and operational applications, the conversation around context needs to change. We have become accustomed to asking whether a model has enough information, whether retrieval is accurate, and whether its context window is large enough. Those questions remain important, but they are incomplete when the model can initiate actions in an external system. For blockchain-connected agents, a more useful set of questions is:

These are not merely questions about prompt construction. There are questions about data integrity, state management, authorisation, and distributed execution. I see this as an important direction for production AI engineering. As agents become more capable, the surrounding infrastructure must become better at distinguishing information that is useful from information that is safe to act upon. Blockchain makes that distinction particularly consequential because the agent's decisions may result in financial transactions that cannot simply be undone.

The objective should not be to eliminate every delay or force every workflow to wait for the strongest possible confirmation. Different applications have different requirements, and latency, cost, and safety will always need to be balanced. The objective is to make those trade-offs explicit, measurable, and enforceable. An AI agent should know when its information is sufficient to proceed, when its assumptions need to be refreshed, and when uncertainty is too high to justify an action. The real challenge is not teaching an AI agent to understand blockchain data. It is building a system that knows when that understanding is no longer safe to trust. That is where context engineering becomes an essential part of blockchain security, and where reliable autonomous systems will have to prove themselves.

Human approval is not a security boundary unless it is bound to the exact action being approved, enf

AI Engineer and Enterprise Architect passionate about building scalable AI systems and production-ready agentic platforms. I write about AI.
