#9708. Why SSH Still Matters After More Than 30 Years

Imagine managing a server located thousands of miles away. You need to update its software, investigate an application failure, or change a configuration file. You cannot physically access the machine, but you still need to work with it almost as if it were sitting on your desk.

Today, this is a completely ordinary task. Engineers connect to remote servers, execute commands, transfer files, and maintain infrastructure from practically anywhere in the world. Much of this is possible because of a technology called SSH, or Secure Shell.

SSH is one of those technologies that most people outside the IT industry have probably never heard of, even though it plays an important role in the systems they use every day. Websites, banking platforms, cloud applications, and enterprise services all depend on infrastructure that is frequently managed through SSH.

What makes SSH particularly interesting is its longevity. The protocol was introduced in 1995, when the internet was a very different place. Yet, more than three decades later, SSH remains an essential tool for software developers, system administrators, DevOps engineers, and security professionals.

To understand why it has survived for so long, it is worth looking at the problem it was originally designed to solve, how its security mechanisms work, and how its role has changed as computing has evolved.

At its simplest, SSH is a network protocol that allows two computers to communicate securely over a potentially untrusted network. The most familiar use case is remote terminal access. A user opens a terminal, connects to another computer, and begins executing commands.

This command asks the SSH client to connect to a remote machine at the specified IP address using the username admin. If authentication succeeds, the user can work with the remote system through a command-line session. But SSH is much more than a remote terminal protocol. It can also transfer files, execute individual commands, carry application traffic through encrypted tunnels, and provide secure authentication for automated processes.

The importance of SSH comes from three fundamental security properties:

Confidentiality means that network traffic is encrypted so that someone intercepting the communication cannot easily read its contents.

Integrity means that the receiving system can detect unauthorized changes to transmitted data. An attacker should not be able to modify commands or responses without the modification being detected.

Authentication helps establish that the client is communicating with the intended server and that the user attempting to access the server has appropriate credentials.

These properties work together. Encryption alone would not be enough if an attacker could impersonate the destination server. Similarly, verifying a user's identity would provide limited protection if commands and passwords were transmitted openly.

One of the most interesting aspects of SSH is how much happens before the user sees a command prompt. Typing a simple SSH command starts a sequence involving network communication, cryptographic negotiation, identity verification, session-key generation, and user authentication. Understanding these steps helps explain why SSH is considered secure and where configuration mistakes can introduce risks.

SSH normally operates over TCP, using port 22 by default. The client first establishes a TCP connection with the server. TCP provides a reliable communication stream, ensuring that data is delivered in order and that lost segments can be retransmitted.

At this point, the connection itself is not yet protected by SSH encryption. The client and server then exchange protocol identification strings, which indicate the SSH protocol versions and software implementations they support. A server might identify itself with a string similar to:

This tells the client that the server implements SSH protocol version 2. The version exchange is followed by negotiation of the cryptographic algorithms that will be used during the session.

SSH does not depend on a single encryption algorithm. Instead, the client and server each advertise supported algorithms and select compatible choices. These choices include algorithms for key exchange, server authentication, symmetric encryption, and message integrity.

Modern SSH implementations may use algorithms such as:

These algorithms serve different purposes.

For instance, public-key cryptography helps authenticate identities and establish cryptographic secrets, while symmetric cryptography handles the continuous flow of data after the session has been established.

This distinction is important because asymmetric cryptographic operations are generally more computationally expensive than symmetric encryption. Rather than encrypting every terminal command with a public key, SSH uses key exchange to establish session secrets and then employs efficient symmetric encryption for the actual communication.

The next challenge is creating encryption keys that both computers can use without exposing those keys to observers on the network. Traditionally, SSH has accomplished this through mechanisms such as Diffie-Hellman or elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

The basic principle is that the client and server exchange mathematical values that allow them to calculate a common secret independently. The secret itself is not transmitted directly. An attacker who captures the publicly exchanged values should not be able to reconstruct that secret under the security assumptions of the selected algorithm. SSH then uses the agreed secret, together with other values from the handshake, to derive cryptographic keys for the session.

Modern algorithms can also provide forward secrecy. Forward secrecy means that obtaining a server's long-term private key at a later date should not, by itself, allow an attacker to decrypt previously recorded sessions. This matters because attackers sometimes store encrypted network traffic in the hope of decrypting it in the future.

However, secure key exchange alone does not prove that the client is connected to the correct server. That requires a separate authentication mechanism.

Every properly configured SSH server has a host identity represented by one or more cryptographic key pairs. During key exchange, the server uses its host private key to sign information associated with the handshake. The client verifies the signature using the server's public host key. This demonstrates that the server possesses the corresponding private key, but another question remains: is this public key really associated with the intended server?

SSH clients commonly maintain a file called known_hosts, usually located inside the user's .ssh directory. When connecting to a server for the first time, the client may display the server's host-key fingerprint and ask whether to trust it. After the key is accepted, it is stored for future comparisons.

On subsequent connections, the client checks whether the presented host key matches the previously trusted identity. If the key changes unexpectedly, the client can display a prominent security warning.

This mechanism helps protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, where an attacker attempts to impersonate the destination server. There is one important limitation: accepting an unknown host key without verifying its fingerprint can establish trust in the wrong machine. Organizations can reduce this risk by distributing verified host keys or using SSH host certificates.

Once the secure transport has been established and the server's identity has been checked, SSH authenticates the user. SSH supports several authentication methods, including passwords, public-key authentication, and additional mechanisms configured by the server.

Public-key authentication is especially common in professional environments. To use it, a user generates a key pair consisting of a public key and a private key.

The public key can be installed on a server, commonly in the user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file.

The private key remains on the user's device and should be protected from unauthorized access.

During authentication, the client uses the private key to create a digital signature over session-specific authentication data. The server verifies that signature using the corresponding public key and checks whether that identity is authorized. If the verification succeeds and the server's authentication policy is satisfied, access is granted.

The important point is that the private key is never sent to the server. The client proves possession of the private key by producing a valid signature. This makes public-key authentication particularly useful for automated systems, because it avoids repeatedly transmitting reusable passwords.

However, the private key still needs protection. If it is stolen and is not sufficiently protected, an attacker may be able to impersonate the user.

After successful authentication, the client can request a terminal session, execute a command, open a file-transfer subsystem, or establish another supported connection channel. For an interactive terminal, the server normally starts the user's shell or another configured command. From this point onward, terminal input and output travel through the SSH encrypted transport.

When the user types a command, the client packages the data into SSH messages, encrypts and authenticates them, and transmits them to the server. The server checks the integrity of the incoming data, decrypts it, and passes the relevant content to the destination process.

Responses travel back using the same general mechanism in the opposite direction, with separate cryptographic keys and state. A network observer can usually still identify the participating IP addresses, connection timing, and approximate traffic volume. However, with properly configured modern algorithms, the observer cannot read the commands or responses.

SSH can also periodically perform a new key exchange during an existing session, a process called rekeying. This limits the amount of traffic protected under a single set of session keys.

Although SSH often appears to be a single protocol, SSH-2 is organized into three major layers.

The transport layer establishes secure communication. It handles cryptographic negotiation, server authentication, encryption, integrity protection, and key exchange.

Above it, the user authentication layer determines whether the connecting client is authorized to access the requested account or service.

Finally, the connection layer manages the actual activities taking place inside the secure transport.

One particularly useful feature of the connection layer is multiplexing. SSH can carry multiple logical channels over a single encrypted connection. For example, a single SSH transport may carry an interactive terminal while also supporting forwarded TCP connections or other permitted channels.

This separation makes SSH much more flexible than a protocol designed only for remote command execution. The same security foundation can support several different kinds of applications without each application having to implement its own encryption and authentication mechanisms.

SSH has become an essential technology across modern IT infrastructure. Although it was originally developed for secure remote access, it now supports a wide range of activities, from software development to infrastructure automation.

Server and Cloud Infrastructure Management

SSH allows engineers and system administrators to securely access remote servers, execute commands, troubleshoot problems, and manage systems hosted in cloud platforms such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Software Development and Git Repositories

Developers use SSH to securely interact with Git repositories hosted on platforms such as GitHub and GitLab. It enables authentication using cryptographic keys, making everyday operations like cloning repositories, pushing code, and pulling updates more convenient and secure.

SSH is widely used in automated deployment and configuration management. Tools such as Ansible rely on SSH to execute commands, install software, and manage large numbers of servers without requiring manual intervention.

Protocols and tools such as SFTP and SCP use SSH to securely transfer files between computers. They are commonly used for backups, application deployments, and exchanging sensitive information between systems.

SSH can create encrypted tunnels that allow applications to communicate securely with remote services. This is particularly useful for accessing databases, internal applications, and other resources that are not directly exposed to the internet.

Network administrators use SSH to configure and maintain routers, switches, firewalls, and other networking devices. It is also widely supported by embedded Linux systems, including Raspberry Pi devices.

SSH is sometimes confused with other security technologies, particularly HTTPS and VPNs. All three can protect network communication, but they serve different purposes.

HTTPS is primarily designed to secure communication between clients and web services using HTTP over TLS. It is the technology that protects ordinary web browsing and many web APIs.

A VPN creates a protected connection that can carry traffic for a wider range of network applications, depending on its design and configuration. It is often used to provide remote access to private networks or to connect separate networks.

SSH, by contrast, is primarily designed around secure remote access, authenticated sessions, command execution, file transfer, and application tunneling.

For example, a software engineer might use HTTPS to access a monitoring dashboard, a VPN to reach an organization's internal network, and SSH to investigate a particular Linux server. These technologies are not necessarily alternatives. They are often used together. An SSH session may run through a VPN, while the server being administered hosts applications that communicate with users over HTTPS. Understanding their different responsibilities is important when designing secure infrastructure.

SSH has an excellent reputation, but it is not a universal solution to every security problem.

One of its limitations is that encryption protects data during transmission, not necessarily after it reaches its destination. If the remote server has already been compromised, an encrypted SSH connection does not prevent an attacker controlling that server from observing commands or accessing data available to the session. Similarly, if a user's private key or workstation is compromised, an attacker may be able to initiate legitimate-looking SSH connections.

SSH also does not automatically provide detailed accountability for every action taken during a session. A server may log the fact that a user authenticated, but reconstructing every interactive command and its effects may require additional auditing or session-recording mechanisms.

There are operational limitations as well. Managing SSH access across a handful of servers is relatively straightforward. Managing it across tens of thousands of servers, contractors, automated workloads, and changing cloud environments is considerably more difficult. Organizations need reliable processes for granting access, revoking credentials, controlling privileges, and monitoring unusual activity.

This is why SSH increasingly operates alongside identity-management systems, access gateways, configuration-management platforms, and security-monitoring tools. Its cryptographic design remains important, but maintaining the security of the surrounding environment is equally essential.

It is easy to overlook foundational technologies because they become part of everyday routines. For an experienced engineer, opening an SSH session may take only a few seconds. The command is familiar, the connection is established, and attention immediately shifts to the task on the remote machine. Yet behind that ordinary interaction is an enormous amount of engineering. The client and server negotiate compatible algorithms, establish cryptographic secrets, verify identities, authenticate the user, and maintain an encrypted communication channel. All of this happens with very little visible complexity.

SSH also demonstrates an important principle in software architecture: well-designed technologies can remain useful long after the environments in which they were created have changed. When SSH first appeared, cloud computing did not exist in its modern form. Containers, Kubernetes, GitHub, and today's automated deployment platforms were still years away.

Nevertheless, the fundamental need for secure communication between computers remained the same. The protocol was designed around that need rather than around one particular product or infrastructure model. As a result, SSH could be adapted to new environments without losing its core purpose.

Today, it connects developers to cloud servers, supports automated operations, secures file transfers, enables controlled access to internal services, and helps administrators manage critical systems. It is not always visible to end users, and it is rarely the technology that attracts attention during major software announcements. But when a production system fails or an engineer needs access to a remote machine, SSH is often one of the first tools they reach for.

SSH started with a relatively simple problem: how to access a remote computer without exposing sensitive information to anyone who could observe the network. Its solution became much more than a secure replacement for Telnet.

Over the following decades, SSH evolved into a versatile protocol supporting remote administration, authentication, file transfers, tunneling, automation, and large-scale infrastructure operations. Its lasting importance comes from the combination of security, flexibility, interoperability, and practical usefulness.

At the same time, SSH reminds us that strong cryptography does not remove the need for proper system administration. Key management, access control, endpoint security, and regular maintenance remain critical to protecting the systems that depend on it.

More than 30 years after its introduction, SSH continues to serve as a trusted foundation for secure remote access. And as infrastructure becomes increasingly distributed, automated, and interconnected, that fundamental capability is unlikely to become less important.

#9707. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9704. Learjet Crash Has Brought The Conspiracy Crowd Out of The Woodwork

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

Australian technology news journalist. Matt, 20 years of IT systems & networking engineering + security turned Journo.

Apparently, it was a missile, the government was involved, and the lack of easily recognisable aircraft parts on the ground proves something sinister happened.

Then came the YouTubers comparing the wreckage to the September 11 attack on the Pentagon and the lack of visible aircraft parts, as though putting two crash videos beside each other amounts to an investigation.

These are the kinds of statements I’ve been reading on social media following the Learjet crash in Florida, and the confidence behind them is extraordinary.

Fly-by-night conspiracy theorists have been announcing their conclusions while investigators are still recovering evidence.

People who appear to have little understanding of aviation are presenting themselves as authorities on aircraft structures, impact damage and the circumstances of the crash.

I’ve been around aviation my entire life, and watching this nonsense circulate is infuriating. Someone sees footage they don’t understand, decides the wreckage looks wrong and immeditely starts suggesting a government opration.

The Pentagon comparisons are particularly tiresome. Comparing the appearance of two crash sites cannot establish what happened at either one without examining the aircraft, impact conditions, structures and physical evidence.

Yet these videos invite viewers to treat their own unfamiliarity with aircraft accidents as proof that something has been concealed.

What makes this behaviour so callous is that real people died. They had families and futures, including a 20-year-old pilot whose aviation career had barely begun.

Imagine losing someone you love, then opening social media to find strangers using their final moments to promote an unsupported missile theory.

The aircraft was a Learjet 60, registered N722BD, flying from Austin towards the Bahamas. Flight tracking information and cockpit transmissions document a weather encounter followed by a catastrophic descent near West Palm Beach on 1 November.

The crew reported icing, turbulence and precipitation before reporting an overspeed condition during the descent.

There is meaningful information to examine, but apparently that requires more effort than typing “government cover-up” beneath a video.

My own assessment, based on the information available, is that this looks like poor navigation and possible pilot error during a dangerous weather encounter. That remains my interpretation, subject to the investigation establishing what happened.

The sequence I consider plausible is that icing contributed to an aerodynamic stall and loss of control, followed by a rapidly accelerating descent and structural damage.

Ice forming on the wings, including around their leading edges, can disrupt airflow, reduce lift and increase stall speed. The FAA describes these effects in its guidance on airframe icing.

If sufficient ice accumulated on this aircraft, it could have contributed to a stall and the subsequent nose-down descent.

Investigators will need to establish whether that occurred, how the ice protection systems were operating and what other factors affected the aircraft.

At the reported altitude, temperatures around minus 40 degrees Celsius are conceivable, although altitude alone cannot establish the actual outside air temperature.

Extreme cold also needs to be understood properly: conventional airframe icing depends on supercooled liquid water, which approaches its theoretical freezing limit around minus 40 degrees Celsius.

The crew’s reported icing encounter deserves serious examination. It doesn’t give any of us permission to declare the complete accident sequence proven.

During the extreme descent, increasing speed and aerodynamic loads may have caused part of the tail to separate. Losing an essential pitch control surface would make recovery impossible, depending on the damage and the aircraft’s condition.

Investigators recovered three pieces of the left elevator between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site. They have yet to establish whether its separation contributed to the initial loss of control or resulted from forces acting on the aircraft during the descent.

That is a serious question involving physical evidence. It deserves considerably more attention than someone’s unsupported claim about a missile.

Then there’s the supposedly devastating observation that you “can’t see any aircraft parts on the ground”.

What exactly were these people expecting to see? A smashed up fuselage beside the road, complete with wings and a registration conveniently facing the camera?

Given the aircraft’s mass and impact speed, extensive fragmentation is a credible explanation for why little in the footage resembled a recognisable aircraft.

A violent impact can break an aircraft into small pieces, with wreckage scattered, buried or damaged by fire.

An aircraft striking the ground at close to the speed of sound would carry enormous kinetic energy because of its mass and velocity, potentially comparable to several tonnes of TNT. The impact could reduce much of it to tiny fragments, leaving little recognisable as an aircraft, being effectively “atomised”.

The recovery of aircraft components already undermines the assertion that there was no plane. Failing to identify wreckage in a video says little about what investigators can recover from the scene.

What amazes me is how quickly a lack of knowledge becomes absolute certainty. Someone doesn’t understand the wreckage, so the wreckage must be suspicious. A detail is missing from an early report, so someone must be hiding it.

These people then demand that everyone else disprove whatever they’ve imagined.

I’m prepared to explain what I consider plausible and acknowledge where the evidence remains incomplete. If the investigation establishes a different cause, my assessment will have to change.

Anyone alleging a missile strike or government involvement should bring evidence capable of supporting that accusation. A YouTube comparison with the Pentagon and a comment about missing wings won’t do it.

Nine people died, and their families are now living with that loss. Before posting another smug declaration about what “really happened”, perhaps these self-appointed investigators should consider whether they would repeat it while standing in front of those families.

#9702. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9697. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9695. “Move Fast and Break Things” Is Dead. What Counts in Enterprise AI Now?

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The invoices are ending Silicon Valley’s favorite motto that built the AI boom.

Right before Facebook went public, Mark Zuckerberg shared the “move fast and break things” motto in his 2012 letter to investors. The idea was to build and launch quickly, fix problems later, and learn from mistakes. Startups across Silicon Valley embraced this approach. During the web and mobile boom, the focus was on gaining users first, with monetization, compliance, and governance left for later. When ChatGPT entered the market, the industry repeated this strategy on a larger scale. Companies scrambled for computing power and began spending heavily on licenses, pilots, and APIs, treating AI as a land grab.

At Facebook’s developer conference in April 2014, Zuckerberg joked about a new motto: “move fast with stable infra.” With 1.28 billion users, breaking things had become expensive.

The motto worked until mistakes became more expensive because of the token costs, and the results stopped matching expectations. In a PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs, 56% said they had seen no significant financial benefit from AI so far.

Costs have also been harder to predict than anyone planned. A Harness study found that 72% of organizations had had an unexpected AI cost spike, and more than half said no one clearly owns AI spending. Harness sells AI cost-management software, so it has a stake in how big the problem looks. Cloudera’s research points to another problem: segmented data systems and silos make it hard for companies to measure what AI really costs them to run.

In April, Uber’s CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga said the company had used up its entire 2026 AI budget after just four months of Claude Code. Teams had been ranked on an internal leaderboard by how much AI they used. By June, the company limited each employee to $1,500 a month per AI coding tool. In August, Naga wrote that Uber was coming to the end of the so-called “tokenmaxxing era,” when burning tokens meant productivity.

Gartner's advice to CFOs is to treat AI cost as an architecture issue rather than a budget line item. One unmonitored prompt library alone can "risk running up millions of dollars in additional expense".

That’s the new rule. Finance asks the question nobody asked loudly in 2023: what did we get?

Finance teams can't parse a transformer model, but they can easily understand a unit price. Unit price is now the driver of architecture decisions. So how do you deal with that?

Route tasks wisely. Don’t just send every job to the largest model. In his annual letter on October 21, 2026, Satya Nadella introduced the “cost-to-outcome” frontier: “After all, Super Intelligence is changing every organization’s inputs (how they work) as well as their outputs (the products and services they sell). At the same time, inference is making marginal cost an important factor in software economics as usage scales. As a result, customers will increasingly measure the cost of tokens against the outcomes they produce. We call this the “cost-to-outcome” frontier, and we are focused on optimizing it.”

For engineers, that means sending classification, extraction, and summarisation to a smaller, cheaper model, caching repeated prompts, and using the frontier model only for the work that needs it.

Count everything. FinOps for AI is the top priority in the State of FinOps 2026 Report, and AI expense management is a skill teams currently need to build. In practice, that means tagging every model call by team and feature and giving each agent its own budget and alert, so a runaway loop triggers an alarm before it reaches the invoice.

A new software market is emerging to meet this demand. Max Gontar, CEO of the AI-powered finance software company Kairos, explains:

The first wave of enterprise AI was all about wild spending on experiments in the hope of seeing what the models could write/generate. The current state is that CFOs are getting what they actually need: software that runs within their existing infrastructure to find working capital leaks, deliver tangible ROI and automate finance workflows as a result (that's where AI really is good at). The new challenge for the CFO is the management of AI infrastructure spend. They now have to work out how many tokens it makes sense to spend on each process, what to cut and what to rebuild. The ROI of every function in the business will be more transparent than it's ever been.

Watch who owns the numbers. In the FinOps Foundation’s 2026 survey of 1,192 practitioners, 78% of FinOps teams report to the CTO or CIO, and only 8% report to the CFO. So finance didn’t take control, but it did get veto power. The CFO asks, “What did this return?” and engineering manages the dashboard with the answer.

There’s a problem, though. If every task has to meet a cost limit, who pays for work you can’t predict? Cost-to-serve metrics reward what’s measurable now, but exploration usually isn’t measurable in the short term.

There's no 2026 data at all to show that cost discipline is in any way reducing the amount of exploratory research so it's a valid concern rather than a fact. The moral guidelines, the risk frameworks, the ethical manifestos all sit in a PDF somewhere and are presumably being read. A runaway agent loop doesn't do that. It shows up as a number on a bill and numbers get attention. The ledger will only protect what it can count.

Here's the obvious objection: if the era is over why are the giants still throwing money at it? Forbes has the four biggest spenders (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet) at $700-$725bn of capital expenditure in 2026, up 75% on $410bn in 2025.

This only makes the argument clearer. The sellers are the hyperscalers. They build capacity and fund it with huge cash flows, betting on future demand. Their customers are the buyers, and buyers pay attention to invoices. If a buyer cuts back, chooses cheaper models, or limits usage, it affects the demand that sellers are counting on.

There's a bit of a tension there. Capacity is being built on the basis that the enterprises will be spending a lot more, whilst the same enterprises are in fact capping their usage, moving to cheaper models and asking what they got for the money. One side of that equation is either completely wrong or just way ahead of its time.

Facebook abandoned 'move fast and break things' when it started to get expensive. A decade on and enterprise AI is running into the same wall, just with a much bigger bill. It's not over yet. Finance has the veto, they just can't yet see what they're giving up in terms of accuracy and ambition. 'Move fast and break things' died because of the invoices. The next battle is over what gets counted.

#9692. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9689. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9687. osFoundry 的 Agent team 能做什麼？什麼時候一個 agent 就夠了？

星期二早上 7:40，Priya 手上有個問題，主管要她午餐前給答案：一週工作四天，產出真的不會掉嗎？她大可以把問題貼進聊天機器人，拿回一段口氣篤定的文字。但找數字的模型，同時也是判斷這些數字站不站得住腳的模型，而它很少會反駁自己。她要的是一個人去找試行案例、另一個人把數據拉出來，再由第三個人把沒有來源的東西全部退回去。

osFoundry 是一款在自己電腦上跑 AI 工作的桌面應用程式，把工作交給 agent 的方式有兩種，兩者關係很近。Agent（側邊欄顯示為 Single agent）是一個有名字、只負責一件事的 agent：你給它指示，它會拿到自己的 ID，例如 AG-0001L，每一次執行都有紀錄，之後可以回頭追。Agent team 則是讓一位 leader 帶著一組專職成員。Leader 規劃工作、把每個步驟分給成員，再由 reviewer 檢查每一步，通過後才會交到你手上。兩者都在側邊欄的 Agents 底下，緊鄰彼此，開啟的也是同一個畫面。差別只在成員多寡。如果你待過有專案經理的群組聊天，Agent team 用起來會很熟悉。不同的是，每則訊息、每次交接、每個判定都會留下來，可以捲回去看。

Priya 打開 Agent team，按下 New session。在 New team session 對話框裡，她維持「Start from a team」，並從 Team 清單選了 Deep Research Team。對話框載入了五位成員（deep-research-agent、research-analyst、data-researcher、search-specialist、academic-researcher）。「Who leads」底下顯示 Orchestrator，說明是「plans the work up front, then delegates the steps to the agents below」。她也可以在任何一位成員上按「make leader」，改由那位成員帶頭。

她按下 Create，在 leader 的聊天裡輸入問題送出。Leader 把問題拆成五個部分：找試行案例、找研究、找數字、找反面證據，最後整合成一個答案。三位成員同時開工。Data Researcher 會先等 Search Specialist 的清單出來，才開始拉數據。當 Data Researcher 回報一個 40% 的數字時，reviewer 把它標成「Sent back」，理由是沒有來源、日期也沒有衡量指標。這一步重新執行、找到來源，然後通過。

最後她在中間窗格拿到一個答案，裡面每個數字都經過「找到它的 agent 以外」的人檢查。她還拿到一行誠實的「Not covered」，可以直接貼進給主管的筆記。

Tom 一週會好幾次把會議紀錄整理成待辦事項，每次都得先把同一段規則貼進聊天裡。這種工作不需要團隊，需要的是一個記得規則的 agent。

他打開 Single agent，按 New session，停留在 Create in chat 分頁。在「New agent」欄位寫一行說明需求，按下 Start。打開的聊天是一個設定用的 agent。它問了幾個問題，接著提出名稱、@handle 和完整的指示。輸入框上方會出現一張卡片，上面有名稱、handle、Show instructions 連結和 Create agent 按鈕。

他打開指示，確認他最在意的那條規則有寫進去：絕對不要猜負責人或截止日。然後按下 Create agent。同一個聊天現在就變成那個 agent。他貼上會議紀錄後，缺少的負責人和日期都會標示為缺漏，絕不會用猜的。這個工作階段會在側欄保留它的 Agent ID，下次他只要選這個 agent 就好。

Dari 負責一個小型產品團隊的發版。她的團隊工作階段有一位 leader，成員是 Release Drafter、Change Auditor、Docs Reviewer、QA Summarizer 和 Approval Prep，各自負責發版包的一部分。

執行之前，她打開 Goal 分頁，按下 Set a goal。面板說明，目標會拆成幾條成功條件，一開始都是失敗，隨著 agent 達成逐一轉綠。工作階段會持續執行，直到全部通過或達到回合上限。她寫了三條條件，最後一條是核准資料包要齊全。成員工作時，她在 Handoffs 追蹤從 leader 到各成員再回來的整條鏈。她也會看 Proposals 裡有沒有成員提出的設定變更，那裡的東西沒有她點頭都不會套用。她隨時可以在 leader 的聊天裡回覆來調整方向，審閱時也可以按面板標題列的 Pause 暫停執行。

最後她拿到發版包，以及每個部分由誰起草、誰稽核、誰核准的紀錄。有人問 release notes 裡某一行是怎麼來的，她都能拿出來給對方看。

Agent 和 Agent team 是工作的起點，Sessions 則是你觀察工作的地方。這個看板把每個聊天、agent、團隊和終端機工作階段都顯示成一張卡片，依照工作階段實際的狀態分到 Running、Needs you、Paused、Idle、Done 和 Failed。

同一份團隊工作需要反覆執行時，Loop 會替成員名單加上觸發條件、上限，以及每一回合哪些條件通過的紀錄。Graphs 則適合路徑會依中途結果而改變的工作。與 leader 的對話是一個 Maestro 聊天，所以團隊的答案可以接著用在你其他的 Maestro 工作裡。工作階段的 Enable sync 連結會把它接上專案的訊息頻道，讓人和 agent 在同一個地方溝通。更多內容請看 Agents 功能頁面 和 agent 工作階段概覽。

什麼時候該用單一 agent，而不是團隊？ 工作是一件明確、規則固定的任務時，用單一 agent，例如整理筆記格式，或用同一種語氣草擬回覆。工作包含需要不同工具的幾個部分，或你希望在看到結果前先由另一位 reviewer 把關時，就用團隊。

工作階段開始後可以換團隊嗎？ 不行。New team session 對話框寫明團隊「is fixed for this session's life」。在按下 Create 之前，你仍可以在對話框裡新增或移除 agent、選擇由誰帶頭。要換成其他成員名單，就開一個新的工作階段。

這些東西有任何部分在雲端執行嗎？ New session 表單提供 Local 和 Isolated 兩種執行方式。表單上註明兩者都用你自己的金鑰在你的電腦上執行，不會有任何東西送到雲端。聊天紀錄預設存在本機。

Agent 可以改寫自己的指示嗎？ 它們可以提出修改建議，建議會出現在 Proposals。提案不等於已接受的設定。Agent 能不能動到自己的 prompt，是另一個獨立的設定。

#9686. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:
