#9684. Google's 2027 LSA Expansion Has an API Availability Problem

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Google's planned 2027 expansion of Local Services Ads (LSAs) creates an important technical question for agencies and software providers: will Google Ads API capabilities expand at the same pace as the advertiser migration?

Google's migration roadmap says non-US accounts and remaining business categories will transition to Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in 2027. Yet the current Google Ads API documentation still restricts the country_code field for these campaigns to US.

This is not proof that international API support will arrive late. Google may update its API documentation and regional capabilities before the relevant migration phases begin. But it exposes an integration risk that agencies should address before international accounts move into the new campaign architecture.

The issue is bigger than campaign creation. It affects account provisioning, location validation, campaign automation, conversion-goal configuration, reporting, and the ability to manage multiple markets through a single software layer.

Google is moving LSAs into a specialized Performance Max campaign structure while retaining the pay-per-lead model and local placements on Search and Maps.

Its published migration schedule has three broad phases:

August 2026: selected US home and storefront services

Late 2026: broader advertiser groups, including service-area businesses and professional services

2027: non-US accounts and remaining supported categories

The API documentation describes a more limited geographic capability at present. The Performance Max for pay-per-lead setup requires a two-letter country code in local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.country_code, and the documented supported value is US. The documentation also states that location criteria must belong to the campaign's home country.

That creates a distinction between two forms of availability:

These capabilities are related, but they are not interchangeable. A campaign becoming available in the Google Ads interface does not automatically establish that every API workflow, field, validation rule, or regional dependency is available too.

Sources: Google Ads API: Performance Max for pay-per-lead goals and supported business verticals.

Consider an agency managing campaigns for plumbing businesses in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

A conventional campaign-management platform might represent each account using a shared configuration:

This is a simplified internal representation, not a Google API request.

The problem emerges when the provisioning service translates that configuration into Google's campaign resource. If the API validates the country code against the currently supported value of US, an international campaign cannot simply be created by substituting GB or AU.

The integration must distinguish between a market supported by the advertising product and one supported by the API provisioning workflow.

A robust system should therefore maintain a capability registry rather than assuming that every market supports every operation.

The values above are illustrative. They should be populated from verified Google documentation and account-level eligibility checks, not treated as Google's published UK capability status.

This registry becomes particularly important during phased rollouts. Different accounts may become eligible at different times, even when they operate in the same country or vertical.

Google's API implementation has also evolved across versions.

The Local Services campaign documentation distinguishes standalone campaigns using:

from Local Services campaigns represented as specialized Performance Max campaigns:

This distinction matters for integrations that identify campaigns by advertising channel type alone.

This is part of a broader API transition problem in Google's LSA migration. As I discussed in The Hidden API Problem in Google's LSA-to-PMax Migration, changes to campaign architecture can create compatibility challenges for agencies that depend on programmatic account management. The 2027 international expansion adds another dimension: regional API availability.

Google's documentation now describes Local Services Performance Max campaign creation and management through the API starting in version v26. Earlier API versions had more limited support, including update-only workflows for eligible campaigns created through the Google Ads interface.

However, API version support and geographic eligibility are separate constraints. Supporting the required resource fields in v26 does not mean every country can use them.

An integration can therefore pass its API-version checks and still fail during campaign creation because a required country, listing, location asset, or account prerequisite is unsupported.

Source: Google Ads API: Local Services campaigns.

Local Services Performance Max campaigns are not configured independently of business-location data.

The API workflow requires a Google Business Profile listing ID through local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.listing_id. Google validates this listing during campaign creation against the associated location assets.

An international rollout may require more than accepting a new country code. It may also require market-specific validation rules, supported location criteria, phone-number formats, language constraints, and business-verification workflows.

For agencies, this means a campaign provisioning system should not treat a Google Business Profile listing ID as a globally interchangeable identifier. It must validate the relationship between the listing, the account, the market, and the campaign before submitting a mutation request.

Local Services Performance Max campaigns use a constrained set of lead conversion categories.

The current API documentation identifies:

For non-coupon campaigns, phone-call leads are automatically configured as the required active goal. Message leads are created but disabled by default. Booking goals depend on an approved Reserve with Google partner being detected on the linked location.

These rules matter because an agency cannot safely assume that a campaign's conversion configuration is identical across every market or account.

A provisioning service should validate the goals returned by the API rather than assuming that a successful campaign creation request means every intended lead channel is active.

It should also separate campaign configuration from actual lead availability. A goal being technically configurable does not guarantee that the underlying service or partner integration is available in a particular market.

Source: Google's pay-per-lead API documentation.

The practical response is to make campaign automation capability-aware.

A single global provisioning workflow is attractive, but it can become fragile when product eligibility, API support, and verification requirements change independently.

A more resilient architecture should include five components:

Maintain a market-level record of supported campaign operations, API versions, verticals, conversion goals, and location requirements. Store the source and date of each capability check.

Before creating a campaign, validate the account's market, business category, Google Business Profile listing, location assets, and required lead goals. Reject unsupported combinations before sending a mutation request.

Keep Google API resource mapping separate from internal campaign models. This makes it easier to handle changes to resource fields, validation rules, and API versions without rewriting the entire agency platform.

Use an internal provisioning state machine to prevent duplicate campaign creation when requests time out or return ambiguous errors. Record the Google resource name and mutation result before retrying.

Track API errors by country, API version, operation, campaign type, and error code. A rise in INVALID_LOCAL_SERVICES_PERFORMANCE_MAX_LISTING_ID errors, for example, should be investigated separately from country-code validation failures.

These controls also make it easier to identify whether a failure comes from account eligibility, API capability, location configuration, or a temporary service issue.

Google's 2027 LSA expansion is a significant platform change, but the most important engineering challenge may be hidden from advertisers. Agencies that depend on API-driven reporting, campaign provisioning, and multi-market automation need to prepare for regional capability differences.

The current documentation establishes a clear constraint: the documented pay-per-lead API workflow is US-specific, while Google's migration roadmap schedules non-US accounts for 2027. Whether those capabilities converge before international migration begins remains something agencies must monitor.

The safest approach is not to build international automation around an assumed rollout date. It is to build systems that can detect regional capabilities, validate account eligibility, and adapt when Google releases new API support.

A global advertising product needs more than a global migration announcement. It needs a globally consistent and documented integration surface.

#9682. Debug della memoria con agenti: come scovare leak in Chrome DevTools (senza impazzire tra snapshot enormi)

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at frontendfacile.it

Dai heap snapshot “a tre scatti” ai percorsi di retainer: un flusso di lavoro pratico per individuare DOM staccati, listener dimenticati, crescita WASM e sprechi di stringhe.

Negli ultimi anni ci siamo abituati a sviluppare come se la memoria fosse una risorsa “comoda”: device potenti, RAM abbondante, framework che astraggono tutto. Poi arriva il conto: UI che diventano viscose dopo qualche navigazione, tab che consumano centinaia di MB, crash apparentemente inspiegabili. La buona notizia è che oggi il memory debugging può essere molto più sistematico (e meno doloroso), soprattutto se deleghi le parti ripetitive a un agente e tieni tu il controllo sulle scelte tecniche.

Di seguito trovi un flusso di lavoro concreto per scoprire leak, capire chi trattiene cosa e arrivare a una fix mirata.

Gli strumenti di memory debugging pensati per lavorare con agenti sono una funzionalità avanzata e si attivano tramite configurazione (tipicamente aggiungendo un flag nel JSON dell’MCP server). L’idea è semplice: le analisi di memoria possono essere “costose” e non ha senso renderle disponibili (e attive) quando non servono.

Operativamente, quando l’abilitazione è corretta, l’agente può usare tool dedicati per:

Il modo più robusto per confermare un leak lato JavaScript rimane il classico metodo a tre snapshot. Funziona bene perché evita falsi positivi dovuti a caching e oscillazioni normali dell’allocazione.

Un heap snapshot è una fotografia della memoria JS in un istante: oggetti, riferimenti, e soprattutto cosa li trattiene.

Scatta un primo snapshot prima dell’azione sospetta.

Esempio: sospetti una perdita quando un componente viene smontato (unmount) o quando cambi route in una SPA.

Forza un GC (dove disponibile) e poi scatta il terzo snapshot: ciò che resta dopo il GC è molto più indicativo.

I file raw degli snapshot sono enormi: ingestibili per un agente e spesso poco pratici anche per una lettura manuale. La differenza la fanno strumenti che trasformano il confronto in un riassunto: l’attenzione va su ciò che cresce davvero in modo anomalo.

Il segnale più utile è la retained size delta positiva: memoria che avrebbe dovuto essere liberata e invece è ancora trattenuta.

Un classico: rimuovi un elemento dal DOM (quindi non è più nella tree), ma esiste ancora un riferimento JavaScript che lo trattiene. Risultato: il nodo non viene garbage-collected.

Nota importante: staccare dal DOM non basta. Il GC non ragiona in termini di DOM visibile, ma di raggiungibilità via riferimenti.

E attenzione anche all’altro lato: a volte mantenere nodi “staccati” è una scelta intenzionale (riuso per performance). Non è automaticamente un bug: lo diventa quando cresce senza controllo e senza limiti.

C’è un equivoco diffuso: “la closure trattiene solo le variabili usate”. In pratica spesso viene trattenuto più contesto del previsto, e basta un singolo oggetto “pesante” nello scope per impedire il rilascio di molta memoria.

Qui l’analisi vincente è il retaining path: partire dall’oggetto che ti aspetti morto (il componente o un suo sub-oggetto) e risalire alla catena che lo mantiene vivo. Quando il colpevole è un riferimento JS diretto, in DevTools spesso lo riconosci anche visivamente nel retainer tree.

Con WebAssembly entri in un modello diverso: la memoria è una linear memory (concettualmente un grande ArrayBuffer). Il garbage collector JS non vede gli oggetti interni (C/C++/Rust) e quindi non può liberare ciò che non liberi esplicitamente.

Anche se non puoi “ispezionare” direttamente le strutture WASM come oggetti JS, c’è un indizio molto forte: l’agente può osservare che il buffer condiviso cresce costantemente. Questo è spesso sufficiente per capire dove indagare:

Non tutti i problemi di memoria sono leak: a volte è spreco strutturale. Un caso sorprendentemente comune è ripetere la stessa stringa in migliaia di oggetti.

Gli strumenti di analisi possono individuare le stringhe duplicate e quantificarne l’impatto, dandoti un bersaglio chiaro.

Quando sospetti un leak reale, questo approccio riduce il rumore:

Il punto non è tornare a programmare come se avessimo pochi kilobyte: è evitare che una SPA moderna si comporti come se potesse consumare tutto senza conseguenze. Con il metodo a tre snapshot, il confronto guidato dalle retained size delta e l’analisi dei retaining paths, puoi trasformare un problema nebuloso (“dopo un po’ rallenta”) in una catena causale verificabile (“questo listener su window trattiene questa closure che trattiene questo componente”).

La ricaduta pratica è immediata: meno tab che esplodono in RAM, UI più reattive e bug più facili da riprodurre e correggere. In produzione, questo spesso vale più di qualsiasi micro-ottimizzazione.

Articolo originale: https://frontendfacile.it/blog/debug-della-memoria-con-agenti-come-scovare-leak-in-chrome-devtools-senza-impazz

#9681. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9679. Closing door prank trend: what it is and how to make your own AI version from one photo

If your TikTok feed has been full of people sprinting down a hallway while a door swings shut, that is the closing door prank (also called the fake closing door prank or door closing prank). It took off at the end of October 2026, and by early November there were AI versions that need only a single photo.

I built a small tool called Turnly that makes these from a photo, so I will say that up front. Below is what the trend is, the three realistic ways to make your own, and the trade-offs of each.

The clip has a fixed shape, which is why it is easy to copy:

Couples posted it on their partners, CapCut tutorials showed how to edit it, and one-photo AI versions followed. Nobody is actually hurt in the AI version: the door swings toward shut and the runner always lands on the near side.

You need a hallway, a door you can close safely, a friend to hold it, and a few takes. It is free and it is the real thing. The downside is that a door closing on a sprinting person is how people get hurt, so keep it slow and padded, or skip it.

Several CapCut tutorials show how to fake the effect from your own clips. CapCut is free to start (check its current plans for the export options you need). You still have to shoot the footage and do the timing by hand, so expect an evening, not five minutes.

An image-to-video model can invent the hallway, the door and the run. You upload one clear photo of the runner (full body works best), and optionally a second photo of whoever closes the door.

This is what Turnly does. On its closing door prank page the moves and timing are already set, so there is no prompt to write:

Limits worth knowing: the hallway and the door belong to the AI, the runner is small at the far end of the hallway at first so the face shows best once they are through the door, and with one photo the person at the door is made up by the AI. It also does not use the trend's original audio, so switch the sound off and add the trend's sound inside TikTok when you post.

Using a TikTok search for "closing door prank ai" and counting different creators whose caption names the trend, I counted 64 creators who posted an AI version in the 7 days to November 5, 2026. Meme trends fade fast, so if you want to join in, do it this week.

If you try any of these, tag the person you would do it to for real. And if you spot something wrong in this write-up, tell me in the comments.

#9677. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9675. Retries Without Double Effects: Idempotency Keys for LLM Tool Calls

An LLM agent decides to call your create_refund tool. The request times out. The agent framework retries, or the model simply asks for the same tool call again on its next turn. Did the customer get one refund or two?

Timeouts don't tell you whether the first attempt ran. That was true for every HTTP client long before LLMs, and the fix is the same: make the side-effecting operation idempotent, so repeating it is safe. What changes with agents is how often the repeat happens and how hard it is to notice afterwards.

There are at least three layers that can repeat a tool call:

Only the first one is usually configured on purpose. The other two show up in logs as "the agent did it twice".

The IETF draft The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field (draft-08, dated 22 October 2026; still an Internet-Draft, not an RFC) describes the common pattern. Its stated aim is to "make non-idempotent HTTP methods such as POST or PATCH fault-tolerant". The client sends a unique key with the request, and the server remembers what happened for that key.

The draft spells out the cases worth handling:

Stripe's Idempotent requests documentation (no date shown; read 2026-11-05) shows one production policy. For its v1 API it says keys are removed after they are at least 24 hours old, and that retries with the same key return the saved response, "including 500 errors". It suggests V4 UUIDs and warns against putting sensitive data such as email addresses in keys.

For agents, the critical question is who generates the key. If the tool wrapper generates a fresh UUID on every call, a model-initiated repeat gets a new key and runs again. The key has to represent the intended effect, decided once.

A practical rule: derive the key when the agent plans the action, store it with the step, and reuse it for every retry of that step. If the model asks for "the same refund" in a later turn, the loop can match it to the existing step instead of minting a new one.

This in-memory version shows the three outcomes. A real one needs a durable store and an atomic "claim" operation.

Being able to tell one decision retried from two decisions made is part of the problem we work on at Obligra. Obligra Verify™ is a system of record for AI-assisted decisions, in public preview, designed to retain the evidence your application selects. The idempotency pattern above is worth adopting regardless of where your records live.

This article was generated by an AI agent (Claude) for the Obligra Verify team and checked against the linked sources.

#9673. The Zero-Budget AI Launch Playbook: 80% of Your Launch Happens Before Launch Day

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Part 1 of 2: How to earn attention from Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt when you have no ad budget

Try this thought experiment. You have a good idea for an AI product. How long before someone else ships something nearly identical?

A year ago the honest answer was a few months. Today, with Claude Code, Cursor and a dozen other tools, it's closer to a long weekend. You can polish the model, sand down the UX, tune the prompts. Competitors can do all of that too, and they'll do it faster than you'd like.

What they can't copy overnight is who already knows you exist: the communities that trust you, the search results that surface you, the people who will say your name when someone asks "what should I use for this?" That's distribution, and it's still stubbornly human work.

I come from a growth background and have worked on go-to-market for several AI products: a music generator, an AI companion app, a financial-data platform, and a few others. I've done launches with money and without it. Some of them worked. Some of them got my accounts banned. This two-part series is the playbook I wish I'd had at the start, with the failures left in.

Part 1 is about the launch itself and the three communities most founders obsess over: Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt. Part 2 covers search, PR, creators and the art of making noise.

When I picture "launching a product," my brain reaches for the standard toolkit: buy promotion, record a slick demo video, line up a wave of creators to post the same demo on the same day with the same script, and manufacture the feeling that this thing is blowing up.

That's a valid playbook, and I'll get to it. But it hides the most important fact about launches: the visible event is the tip of the iceberg.

Take Product Hunt. Whether your product climbs the daily ranking has very little to do with what you do that day. It depends on whether, months earlier, you quietly gathered people who care. We live in an attention economy where everyone is distracted by something else, so the traffic and noise you capture on launch day are a function of the groundwork underneath.

The same goes for offline. A great launch is rarely purely online. It leans on the founder friends you met at a conference, the developers you traded favors with, the investor who happily retweets your news. These threads connect to each other, and none of them can be pulled out of thin air the week before.

So the first reframe: stop asking "how do I launch?" and start asking "what can I build in the 90 days before the launch that makes launch day easy?"

If I could only give you one principle, it would be this: share the value, not your product.

In marketing terms: give first, collect later. Put something genuinely useful in front of people before you ask for anything. Don't expect anyone to use your product in return. They have alternatives, they owe you nothing, and they can smell an agenda from the first sentence.

I'll keep returning to this idea, because it shows up everywhere: in how you post on Reddit, how you write comments, how you build an audience, how you approach creators, even how you make friends at conferences. The tactics change by channel. The rule doesn't.

It also changes how fast you should move. Value-first marketing is slow by design. If you're in a hurry, you'll be tempted to skip straight to the ask, and the channels below are very good at punishing that.

Product Hunt is where most founders start, so let's be honest about what it has become.

The best example I know of a good Product Hunt launch is Gamma, the AI presentation tool. As I remember it, they spent a long time building up a large group of loyal early users before they launched, back when Product Hunt's credibility was still intact. On launch day they rallied those users, and the upvotes were real: actual customers vouching for a product they already liked. That's the model. The ranking was the result of earlier work, not a substitute for it.

Today the picture is murkier, for three reasons:

My suggestion: treat Product Hunt as an optional credibility badge, not your launch. If you already have a base of users who will show up and vouch for you organically, go for it, and choose a calm day. If you don't, spend those weeks building the base.

My team and I have launched on both Product Hunt and Hacker News, and I find Hacker News the more community-driven of the two. It's run by Y Combinator, and it is famously hard to game. If you're thinking about creating a stack of accounts to push a post up the front page, don't bother.

Three things I'd tell anyone planning a Hacker News post:

1. Start building your account months ahead. If you want to share an article or a launch there someday, begin now. Spend three or four months commenting thoughtfully on other people's posts and becoming a recognizable voice. You can't suddenly decide on launch week to do something promotional. The community leans technical and pure, and it reacts badly to anything that smells like marketing.

2. Reputation is what keeps a post alive. If you've made real friends in the community and respected regulars comment on your post, it stays visible far longer. Without that, it sinks quickly.

3. Interesting beats technical. You don't need to publish hardcore engineering to get noticed. When we were working on an AI music product, ChatGPT went down one day. We wrote a song about the outage and shared it. It caught fire on Hacker News, a small but very real win. The bonus came afterwards: a number of people who write technical blogs saw it and linked to our song from their own posts, which handed us several natural backlinks for free.

That last part is worth sitting with. We didn't set out to win backlinks. We made something people wanted to share, and the SEO benefit came as a by-product. That's value-first marketing in miniature.

If you have a small budget or none at all, Reddit is the channel I'd look at first, but only if you can start two to three months early to build up karma and a credible profile.

One warning before the tactics: don't outsource your posts to someone else's accounts. Only the founder really knows what the product feels like, and many "we'll post for you" accounts just generate generic AI-written content that readers sniff out immediately.

Write a genuine comparison of your product and similar tools. Be fair. Cover the pros and cons of your competitors as well as your own, and write as a user of AI tools rather than as the company.

Then post it in small, niche subreddits with a few hundred to a few thousand members, ideally ones whose rules aren't strict about self-promotion. Avoid the giant communities. Their moderators have seen every flavor of disguised promotion and will remove it.

Why bother if the audience is tiny? Because the goal isn't Reddit traffic. It's two long-tail effects:

The mistake people make is wanting both: a comparison post and thousands of eyeballs, so they post it in a huge subreddit and get it removed. Pick one goal.

Posts are slow and risky. Comments are underrated.

This only works if your profile looks like a real community member's and not a billboard. Participate in discussions that have nothing to do with your product.

If you do want to post, make it beneficial to others first. In my experience, the posts that have done well for me, reaching tens of thousands of views and thousands of upvotes, all shared something useful and weren't ads.

Building an AI music product? Share your favorite playlists, artists or recent releases in the right music community. Building an AI travel product? Share routes. Weaving your product into a post in a natural way is tricky, so don't force it.

And here's the pattern that works: be consistent. Post the same kind of thing on a schedule, say one or two playlists a week. For the first four weeks, mention nothing about your product. Let people get used to you as the person who brings good music. Only when the community knows you can you say, "By the way, I'm building this, and it tries to solve that." By then it feels like a friend sharing news.

Reddit communities care deeply about their atmosphere. If people recognize you as someone who adds value, they upvote you and thank you in the comments. If not, you're gone.

The lesson is the one I started with: you can't extract value from a community before you've put some in.

The cheapest launch I've ever run started months before there was a product to launch.

We were building a data platform, something like a Bloomberg-style terminal where people can explore all kinds of data. The question every founder in that position asks is: where do the first users come from?

My answer was to build a media publication in parallel with the product. While the platform was being developed, the publication used its data to write analysis: price trends, macroeconomic outlooks, that kind of thing. Readers found the articles useful enough to forward to friends, and they spread well in several markets. At the bottom of each piece, we invited readers into a private community (a Discord server, for readers outside China).

The whole thing cost almost nothing. It worked because the content and the product were tightly connected: the articles were made from the product's data, so every reader was already a qualified prospect.

If you take one idea from this section, take this: find the valuable thing your product makes possible and give that away publicly, long before you ask for a signup.

Everyone wants the shortcut: the viral post, the front-page ranking, the one tweet that changes everything. Sometimes shortcuts exist. But the launches that hold up are the ones that look like overnight successes and turn out to be slow, boring groundwork on the inside.

Give first. Be patient. Show up in the places where your users already are, as one of them.

In Part 2, I'll cover the other half of the playbook: starting SEO on day one with long-tail keywords, using PR to build authority (including with AI search), working with creators without wasting money, and what to make of the rising wave of attention-grabbing stunts, including the cautionary side of the story.

#9672. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9669. LimeWire AI Studio Review 2023: Details, Pricing & Features

In the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.

As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.

Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.

Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.

The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.

Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.

What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.

The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing users to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.

Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.

Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

#9667. Robots meta vs X-Robots-Tag: why I only use the meta tag

I run a small tool site on plain PHP shared hosting, and one of the smallest decisions I made still shapes how I handle every new page: I control crawlers with a tag in the HTML, and I never touch the X-Robots-Tag HTTP header.

Both do the same job. A robots meta tag lives inside the page and tells a search engine whether to index that page, follow its links, or show a snippet. The X-Robots-Tag does exactly the same thing, but it is sent as an HTTP response header by the server. If you can set headers, the header version is more powerful, because it works on files that are not HTML at all — a PDF, an image, a video. For a page, though, the two are interchangeable, and Google says so plainly.

So why pick one and ignore the other? Because on my setup, headers are work and meta tags are not.

My site is plain PHP pages on shared hosting. There is no framework, no middleware layer, and no single place where every response passes through. To send an X-Robots-Tag I would have to call header() in every PHP file, or add rules to .htaccess that match each URL I want to control. The meta tag, by contrast, goes into the one shared header include every page already loads. One line, one place, done:

And when a page should not be indexed — a thin utility page, a duplicate landing page, a page I only built for a campaign — I change the same line in the same include, or set a variable before the include runs:

That is the whole system. There is no header logic to keep in sync with the markup, and no risk that a header set in one place contradicts a meta tag set in another. When two rules disagree, Google follows the most restrictive one, which is exactly the kind of silent surprise I do not want. One source of truth, in the file I can actually see when I open the page.

There is a second reason, and it is about debugging. When something looks wrong in search results — a page indexed that should not be, a snippet showing text I hid — I can open the page in a browser, view the source, and read the robots instruction right there. A response header is invisible unless I remember to open the network tab or run curl. On a small site run by one person, the thing you can see is the thing you will actually check.

None of this is an argument that the header is bad. If I served PDFs or images I wanted kept out of the index, the meta tag could not help me at all, because a PDF has no to put one in. And on a bigger setup with a framework that sets headers centrally, the header is arguably the tidier choice. But my site serves HTML pages and almost nothing else, and the one non-HTML thing I care about — the download responses — should never be indexed anyway, which I handle by making sure they are never linked as pages.

The lesson is not really about robots at all. On a small project, the best tool is usually the one that lives where you already work. I already edit the shared head include for every page. Putting the crawler instruction there means it gets reviewed every time I touch the page, it cannot drift away from the content it describes, and I never have to remember a second place to look. The header would have been the more "proper" solution. The meta tag is the one that actually gets maintained.

That is the pattern I keep coming back to while building ramrom.io: pick the boring option that lives in one place, and save the clever option for the day the boring one genuinely cannot do the job.

#9665. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9663. The $50 Million Gamble That Made Red Bull Marketing History

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Imagine someone asks you, “Hey, do you want to jump from the edge of space?”

Your first response would probably be, “What the hell is wrong with you?”

But when that exact question was asked to Felix Baumgartner, he basically went, “Yeah, sure. Why not?”

Now, you might be wondering who on Earth was crazy enough to ask that question in the first place.

Ladies and gentlemen, this is the story of the Red Bull Stratos mission: a man crazy enough to jump from the edge of space, a company crazy enough to fund it, and a PR gamble that somehow paid off spectacularly.

Quick disclaimer: Everything you’re about to read comes from me spending the last few hours buried in articles, reports, and marketing resources because apparently that’s what I do for fun now. I tried reading an actual marketing textbook, but it made me question reality, so I fled to Wikipedia, reports, and other resources instead. If I get something wrong, please let me know! Constructive corrections are always welcome—I like learning more than pretending I’m right.

Enough corporate jargon. Let's throw a man out of space.

Now switch the M and the E, and you get Max Emilian Verstappen—okay, that’s not how names work. You get Max Verstappen. But let’s not get distracted.

Earned Media Value (EMV) is the estimated dollar value of publicity a brand receives without paying for it directly.

“The estimated dollar equivalent of unpaid public exposure.”

Which is technically correct, but sounds like a corporate robot wrote it.

So here’s the version my brain understands:

You do something. People can’t stop talking about it. You didn’t pay them to talk about it. That’s EMV.

Influencers posting because they genuinely found something cool? EMV.

People sending the campaign to their friends? EMV.

Yeah... people are definitely going to talk about that.

A simplified formula looks something like this:

EMV = (Total Impressions × Industry CPM) ÷ 1,000

Basically, it estimates how much money the brand would have had to spend on advertising to achieve the same amount of attention.

Some companies also factor in engagement, audience quality, creator influence, and even audience sentiment. After all, ten million people saying, “This campaign is brilliant,” and ten million people saying, “This campaign is terrible,” are two very different outcomes.

Because it lets them estimate the value of all the buzz they generated without paying directly for every conversation.

Imagine your campaign gets millions of people talking. If buying that same amount of attention through traditional advertising would’ve cost millions of dollars, that’s exactly what EMV is trying to estimate.

It isn’t money sitting in Red Bull’s bank account.

It’s simply a way of estimating the advertising value of the attention they earned.

Compared to EMV, ROI is wonderfully straightforward.

ROI simply measures how much profit (or loss) you made compared to how much you invested.

ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Cost of Investment) × 100

Suppose you invest $1,000 into something.

That means your investment generated a 50% return.

A positive ROI means your investment made money.

(Or, as I like to call it, congratulations—you’ve invented a very expensive hobby.)

So what’s the difference between EMV and ROI?

EMV asks: “How valuable was all the attention we earned?”

ROI asks: “Did we actually make money compared to what we spent?”

The other measures financial performance.

We’ll need both of these in a minute because Red Bull Stratos wasn’t just an engineering miracle.

And that's exactly why Red Bull Stratos is still taught as one of the greatest marketing campaigns ever executed.

Somewhere inside Red Bull, on what was probably a completely normal Tuesday, someone had a thought.

A completely normal thought, according to Red Bull standards. Which is already slightly concerning, because Red Bull’s definition of “normal” has historically been questionable.

“Everyone is doing television commercials, right?”

Then came the question that changed everything:

At the time, YouTube livestreaming was still a relatively new idea. Instead of buying a traditional advertising slot, Red Bull could create something people would actively choose to watch.

What could possibly be big enough to capture the world’s attention?

“What if a man jumped from the stratosphere?”

Now, most companies would probably stop here and call it a concerning brainstorming session.

Red Bull looked at the idea and apparently said:

And just like that, Red Bull Stratos was born.

With an estimated investment of around $50 million, Red Bull wasn’t simply funding a stunt. They were funding a scientific mission, an engineering challenge, and one of the boldest marketing gambles in history.

Fifty million dollars is the kind of money that makes normal people rethink buying a coffee.

Red Bull looked at that amount and thought:

“Perfect. Let’s use it to make a human being fall from the sky.”

Unlike certain Formula 1 teams that shall remain unnamed (Ferrari, I’m looking at you), Red Bull actually had a plan.

An Austrian skydiver with years of experience performing extreme jumps, Felix was not exactly someone who looked at a dangerous idea and immediately walked away.

When Red Bull approached him with the idea of jumping from the stratosphere, his reaction was essentially:

Which is either the bravest sentence ever spoken or the sentence responsible for several safety engineers losing sleep.

But this wasn’t just a man standing on a platform and falling.

Behind that jump were scientists, engineers, safety experts, pressure suits, a specially designed capsule, and a massive helium balloon carrying Felix nearly 39 kilometers above Earth.

Basically, hundreds of extremely intelligent people worked together to make sure one person could safely do something that sounded like a rejected cartoon plot.

On October 14, 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped out of his capsule approximately 39 kilometers above Earth.

During his free fall, he reached a maximum speed of around 1,357 km/h, making him the first person to break the sound barrier during a free fall.

The entire event was livestreamed, from the balloon launch to the moment Felix stepped into the unknown.

This was not a commercial people had to sit through before watching something else.

This was the thing people wanted to watch.

The jump itself lasted around 10 minutes, with approximately 4 minutes and 20 seconds spent in free fall before his parachute opened.

What looked like a man simply falling from the sky was actually years of preparation, engineering, testing, and scientific collaboration.

Red Bull had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

But those few minutes had the potential to become one of the greatest marketing successes ever created.

Because this was not a pre-recorded commercial where a company could quietly delete the footage and pretend nothing happened.

And the internet, famously known for being calm and reasonable during unexpected events, was waiting.

If something went wrong, millions of people would see it happen in real time.

Red Bull wasn’t just risking $50 million.

They had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

And then Felix stepped out of the capsule.

At no point during the livestream did Felix stop mid-free fall, pull out a can of Red Bull, take a sip, and say,

“Look at me! I’m literally flying through the stratosphere!”

Because he was wearing a Red Bull-branded pressure suit.

The massive helium balloon carrying him nearly 39 kilometres into the sky?

They didn’t interrupt people’s attention.

Nobody tuned in because they wanted to watch an advertisement.

“Oh my God. Someone is actually going to jump from the edge of space.”

Humans have a fascinating habit of stopping to watch extraordinary things unfold.

When something unbelievable happens, people naturally gather around it.

Instead of asking millions of people to spend thirty seconds watching their advertisement...

...they created something millions of people willingly spent hours watching.

And the brand just happened to own that moment.

Because Red Bull has never really sold caffeine.

They’ve sold the idea that normal is boring.

People don’t buy Red Bull because it’s simply an energy drink.

They buy into everything the brand represents.

Whether that’s Formula 1, cliff diving, mountain biking, air races, or a man casually deciding gravity is optional.

Then the internet did what the internet does best.

Friends sending each other the livestream.

Every conversation became free advertising.

Exactly what we talked about earlier with Earned Media Value.

Nearly eight million people watched simultaneously on YouTube.

Hundreds of millions watched clips afterwards.

The campaign generated an estimated $6 billion in earned media value.

Red Bull didn’t interrupt millions of people to tell them they were exciting.

They did something so exciting that millions of people interrupted their own lives to watch.

How Red Bull Accidentally Built One of the Most Successful Media Empires in Sport

#9661. Google Play In-App Review API: why the card won't show

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at appranker.net

You wired up the Google Play In-App Review API, the task completes without an error, and no rating card ever appears. Usually nothing is broken: the card is quota-limited, the API never tells you what happened, and only one of Google's three test methods shows the real flow. This post gives you a working setup for Kotlin, Expo and Flutter, a rule for when to call it, and a table of the usual reasons the card stays hidden.

The flow is two calls. requestReviewFlow() fetches a ReviewInfo object from Google Play, and launchReviewFlow(activity, reviewInfo) shows a native Play card over your app where the user picks 1 to 5 stars and can add a comment. It runs on Android 5.0 (API 21) and later, including tablets and Google TV, plus ChromeOS, but only where the Google Play Store is installed.

The quota is why Google says not to put the flow behind a button. A user who has used up their quota taps it and sees nothing.

Since each user gets roughly one shot per period, your trigger logic matters more than the integration. Aim for a moment right after the user succeeded at something, while they are between tasks, once they have used the app enough to judge it.

A small eligibility gate keeps calls rare. The thresholds below are an example to tune, not a Google requirement:

Save review_last_asked_at at the moment you launch the flow. You will never learn whether a rating was left, so launch time is the only timestamp you can trust.

Kotlin. Add com.google.android.play:review:2.0.2 (and review-ktx with the same version for Kotlin extensions). Fetch ReviewInfo shortly before the success moment, since it expires after a while:

Errors you may log: PLAY_STORE_NOT_FOUND (-1), INVALID_REQUEST (-2) and INTERNAL_ERROR (-100). Log them, never show them to the user, and wait for the flow to finish before moving to the next screen.

Expo. npx expo install expo-store-review, then check StoreReview.hasAction() before calling StoreReview.requestReview(). Bare React Native apps can use react-native-in-app-review.

Flutter. The in_app_review package gives you both sides:

For a permanent "Rate us" menu entry on Android, link to https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=&showAllReviews=true (or the market:// form) instead of calling the API.

Most "it's broken" reports come from testing in a setup that cannot show a working card.

For the internal test track, all four must hold: the account is on the track, it is the primary account selected in the Play Store, it installed the app from Play, and it has not reviewed the app yet. After that first Play install, you can push new builds from Android Studio and keep testing.

If none fit, check that your eligibility gate ever returns true. A gate that never opens looks exactly like a broken API.

The original covers the policy quotes, the Bare React Native setup and an FAQ in more depth: see the complete Google Play In-App Review API guide for Android, React Native and Flutter. For more on getting your app seen once the ratings come in, browse the AppRanker app leaderboard and ASO guides.

What trigger moment has worked best for your app's review prompt, and did you ever catch it silently burning the quota too early?
