#9603. Skip Salmon: 15 More Sustainable Fish Alternatives

From Japan to New Jersey, salmon is one of the most in-demand, beloved fish in the world, prized for its rich flavor and succulently flaky flesh. But while it's undeniably delicious, there can be some nuances in how sustainable certain varieties are. Sourcing sustainable alternatives can be tricky, but knowing the right certifications and sources can go a long way toward purchasing the right seafood.

Salmon isn't inherently unsustainable, but an incredible amount of global demand can lead to some less-than-ideal practices. In particular, open-net salmon farms may cause environmental issues, whether that's pollution runoff, unsustainable sources of fish feed, or the spread of diseases and parasites to wild populations. One of the biggest differences between farmed and wild salmon is that wild varieties are often more sustainable, depending on the fishery, and well-managed populations are carefully monitored to ensure long-term viability. Still, New Zealand is famous for its highly rated salmon aquaculture, so it would be wrong to paint all farms with the same brush.

When it comes to sourcing other, more sustainable fish, it's often a solid idea to look for something small and fast-growing rather than something large and predatory. While some certifications may greenwash the sustainability of seafood, guidance from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration can help consumers identify responsibly managed fisheries. Despite salmon's unique qualities, there are many fish out there that are more affordable and sustainable and can still be high-quality substitutes in your regular diet.

If you don't want to change up textures and taste, char can be a more sustainable fish with a mild flavor and fewer calories. As a salmonid, it's remarkably similar to salmon and has the same pink flesh, marbling, and savory skin you've already come to love.

Few fish species are quite as environmentally friendly as responsibly sourced sardines, since they're small prey fish that grow quite rapidly in their first years of life. Fresh, dried, frozen, or tinned, sardines come in enough varieties that there's an option for just about everyone.

Freshwater fish get a bad rap for being milder and leaner than ocean-dwelling species, and responsibly farmed rainbow trout is about as tasty and environmentally friendly as it gets. A thick, skin-on fillet cooked with a pat of butter can be just as moist and succulent, and modern farming practices can be quite eco-conscious.

Tasting like someone managed to cross the buttery sweetness of lobster with a fish, sablefish, also known as black cod, is an ocean delicacy. Even well-managed farming operations can have a relatively low environmental impact, particularly when they use responsible feed sources and strict measures to prevent disease.

Essentially just a giant perch, barramundi is a flaky, versatile protein you can prepare exactly the same way you'd cook salmon. They're a unique case in that they're quite large but can thrive on feeds containing plant-based ingredients, so responsibly managed commercial farming operations can have a relatively low environmental impact.

A catfish may not be much to look at, but they're certainly a lot to taste. As bottom-feeders, they can thrive on an omnivorous diet that includes plant-based ingredients, and while they might be a touch lean, few proteins are quite as good when deep-fried or bathed in butter.

One of the mildest fish you can use in just about anything, halibut is a largely sustainable choice, particularly when it's wild-caught in the Pacific. Atlantic populations have faced steep declines from overfishing, so be sure to source it appropriately.

When you're looking for something to bread, batter, or mix into a salad, few types of seafood are quite as good as whiting. Like other fish, however, its sustainability depends on its source, and some well-managed fisheries in U.S. Atlantic waters are more sustainable than those targeting depleted populations elsewhere.

While mahi-mahi sourced from Central America and southern Asia can be a bit problematic, those caught in responsibly managed fisheries in the Atlantic can be quite sustainable. While the fish can reach a respectable 3 feet in length, they grow rapidly, and their populations can recover quite quickly with responsible management.

Snapper is incredibly delicious, but of all the various species, yellowtail snapper from well-managed fisheries can be a particularly responsible choice. Historically, government authorities and local fishers work together to manage certain populations, helping ensure that these fish are harvested responsibly.

Huge, sweet, and oh-so-fun to reel in, the greater amberjack is a common sight for saltwater fishers looking to make tacos or cut thick steaks for the grill. Strict controls over harvesting wild-caught fish can help protect vulnerable populations, although sustainability varies by fishery, so it's worth checking the source before buying it at a seafood counter.

Sometimes called sunshine bass, this hybrid fish is a cross between a saltwater striped bass and a freshwater white bass. These fish grow quickly and tolerate a wide range of conditions, making it relatively easy to raise them sustainably with minimal environmental impact.

Eating carp can not only be sustainable, but buying invasive varieties sourced from the American South can actually be a boon for the environment! Several species of invasive carp have spread through U.S. waterways, so every bite of their earthy, slightly tangy flesh can help support efforts to protect these delicate ecosystems.

Blackened red drum, also called redfish, was once so popular that it prompted an outright commercial fishing ban in federal waters of the Gulf of Mexico. While responsibly farm-raised red drum can still be a sustainable choice, along with certain wild-caught black drum, it's generally still best to avoid wild-caught red drum, as sustainability varies by fishery.

Fresh, clean, and a premium delicacy, grouper can be a gray area of sustainability. While many species, like goliath, Nassau, and Gulf groupers, face serious conservation concerns and may be illegal to harvest in certain areas, responsibly sourced black grouper can be a great substitute for premium-grade salmon.

#9601. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

Hiroshi Sugimoto in the Hirshhorn’s lobby, which he redesigned in 2018 Photo: Farrah Skeiky

When the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden opened in 1974 in Washington, DC, The New York Times called it “the capital’s newest cultural treasure”. Likening the Hirshhorn to a René Magritte picture, reporters drew out the “juxtaposition of man and nature with architecture”, the seamless melding of light and form, indoors and out, that sets apart its collection of Modern and contemporary art.

On 31 October, the Hirshhorn is scheduled to unveil a new cultural treasure: its $68m renovated sculpture garden. The project has been years in the making, designed by the Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto—who also redesigned the museum’s lobby in 2018. The reorganised 1.3-acre space, with its 30,000 new plants and trees, draws on the architect Gordon Bunshaft’s original design. This is part of a broader transformation at the museum, including renovations to the plaza and building infrastructure.

Featuring 60 works—21 of them from the 1974 installation—the renovated garden includes five entrances, east and west overlooks and an underground passageway of stainless steel. Sugimoto describes its mirrored finish as “reflecting the garden and the people moving through it, an experience in itself—one that is continually transformed by the interplay of light, nature and the visitors”.

The walkways and alcoves are delineated using stacked-stone walls, each hand-selected and arranged by the artist. “Bunshaft was deeply influenced by the stone gardens of medieval Japan,” Sugimoto tells The Art Newspaper. “Inspired by this, I decided a Japanese dry-stone wall would serve as a symbolic link between the ancient and the modern, providing the perfect backdrop for the museum’s Modernist sculptures.”

The garden’s opening follows years of controversy. Sugimoto’s early vision for the space was met with criticism. In 2021, Charles A. Birnbaum (the president and chief executive of the Cultural Landscape Foundation) said that the stacked-stone plan “fundamentally disrupts” the garden’s Modernist design and the “artistic intent” of Bunshaft and the landscape architect Lester Collins.

The Hirshhorn’s revamped garden, redesigned by Hiroshi Sugimoto Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Adjustments to Sugimoto’s initial design were made five years ago, according to the Hirshhorn, after a public consultation process as well as meetings with the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts. In 2022, the museum hosted a groundbreaking ceremony with Jill Biden. “I was amazed by the backlash,” Sugimoto said at the time.

Today, Birnbaum stresses that the Hirshhorn’s “landscape architecture is an art form” and urges the museum to “afford it the same curatorial oversight, care and respect as the rest of the material collection”.

Sugimoto’s practice is meditative, rooted in a close study of the natural world. “There is an 11th-century Japanese garden manual, Sakuteiki, which tells us to ‘listen to the voices of the stones’,” he says. Each stone has its own character, weight and direction. He adds: “My task is not simply to place it, but to discover where it already wants to be; precision comes from listening carefully enough to find that inevitable position.”

This sense of balance is felt throughout the garden. With benches for quiet reflection and shaded, out-of-the-way recesses, the lawns encourage deep focus, an attentiveness to and a delight in the play of forms. “It’s not just about looking at art,” says Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s deputy director, “but about looking at it as the garden itself is changing.”

Sculpture in the space is arranged chronologically. The east garden includes a cast of Auguste Rodin’s poignant The Burghers of Calais (1884-89), its six figures weighed down and their necks bound in a darkened procession. Nearby is Henri Matisse’s The Backs I-IV (1909-31), a series of abstracted nudes in bronze relief, their angular silhouettes catching the light.

Auguste Rodin’s The Burghers of Calais (1884-89/cast 1953-59) Photo: Rick Coulby, courtesy Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden

Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952-53) is one of five works by the artist on view. It depicts a pair of seated figures, their faces abstracted, the curve of their shoulders liquid smooth. “Joseph Hirshhorn was one of Moore’s closest friends and one of the most significant collectors of his work,” says Godfrey Worsdale, the director of the Henry Moore Foundation. (Joseph Hirshhorn owned 55 sculptures by Moore, and Hirshhorn’s fourth marriage took place before a cast of the artist’s Upright Motive No. 1: Glenkiln Cross.) Worsdale applauds the renovated garden for offering “unfettered access to Moore’s work for new generations”.

In the west garden, home to new commissions, stands Yoshitomo Nara’s Sentinels of Stillness series (2025)—three monumental heads, fashioned from aluminium and coated in brilliant white paint. Following the Tōhoku earthquake and nuclear disaster in 2011, Nara found himself unable to paint and instead took to sculpting. The physicality of modelling clay served as a kind of healing for him.

Liz Larner’s 6 (2010-11), meanwhile, is a cuboid of stainless steel in deep ochre, lavender and white—the tendril-like lines seeming to expand and contract as if suspended in air. The work is a kind of “variable in space”, says Larner, who is absorbed by the mathematical concept of x (the unknown). Following in the tradition of the Surrealist artist Meret Oppenheim, Larner explores the indefinable, “the variable of a variable, the changing perspectives that don’t ossify”.

Comparably fluid is Raven Halfmoon’s Dancing at Dusk (2024), a neighbouring work of cream, coppery-red and slate-grey travertine. Halfmoon, a citizen of the Caddo Nation, gestures to violence and strength, pairing the themes in a work of banded-stone—her first in the medium—trimmed with a line of crosses. There is a kind of solemnity to the piece, the composite visage resolute, meeting the world as it is.

That pathos carries over to KAWS’s 14ft bronze SHELTER (2026), reminiscent of a mother and child—their eyes crossed out, their modelling soft, even tender. It is a warm embrace, the two encircled by an overhanging elm tree.

There is a stillness to the Hirshhorn’s new garden space, a sense of calm in the otherwise fast-moving capital city. “I hope people will experience a different sense of time in the garden,” Sugimoto says. “The sculptures, stones, trees, water and the changing light all exist on different clocks. The garden allows us to slow our own clock enough to become aware of these differences.”

Critics and city planners question changes to a historic reflecting pool and addition of stacked stone walls in a Modernist environment, while the artist Hiroshi Sugimoto defends his designs but says he is open to negotiating

The artist’s designs for the sunken sculpture park creating a more inviting space for visitors coming from the National Mall

#9597. Skip The McDonald's Egg McMuffin: The Fast Food Breakfast Sandwich With Thick, Crispy Bacon

When it comes to fast food breakfast sandwiches, McDonald's remains uppermost in many people's minds. And why not? The iconic Egg McMuffin, with its famously round egg patty, has been the cornerstone of the chain's breakfast menu since the 1970s. And while you can sub the Canadian bacon that comes standard on the McMuffin for regular bacon, Wendy's Breakfast Baconator actually takes the pork product to a whole new level if that's your sandwich protein preference. And more than that, it ranks as one of the best overall fast food breakfast sandwiches, based on the opinions of the customers who eat them.

Wendy's, which has only served breakfast nationwide on a permanent basis since 2020, is doing the morning meat right with its Breakfast Baconator, which features not only six strips of thick, crispy applewood-smoked bacon, but also a sausage patty — which, like the burgers, comes in a square shape — a freshly cracked egg cooked into a patty (Wendy's is one of the rare fast food chains that use real, whole eggs), two slices of American cheese, and a Swiss cheese sauce. Then, everything gets piled onto not a breakfast bread, like a bagel or English muffin, but a potato roll, which is perhaps better suited to hold the hefty fillings. This symphony of flavors and textures led one user on Reddit to call the immensely bacon-forward sandwich "peak fast food breakfast" that "simply just [can't] get any better," a sentiment echoed by plenty of fellow fans.

The Breakfast Baconator is pretty beloved as-is, but there are ways to modify the menu item and make it that much more enjoyable. One Redditor had the idea of actually stuffing more into the sandwich by adding Wendy's seasoned potato wedges and a flavorful sauce, writing that "it'll change your life." We think the Scorchin' Hot sauce would be an especially tasty addition.

Further, if the potato bun is too lunch-y for you, you can swap it out for a breakfast bread — try asking for the Breakfast Baconator on a biscuit. It's a modification that cannot be made on the app or online, so you'll have to verbally request the change when you place your order at the drive-thru or the counter, if your location still offers that option. Of course, if there simply isn't enough of something on the Breakfast Baconator for your tastes, you can add up to four more sausage patties, four more eggs, and extra Swiss cheese sauce.

#9596. 3 Personality Traits Associated With Infidelity

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner.

People who are low on conscientiousness are more likely to cheat on their partner, research finds.

People who are not conscientious are careless, badly organised and find it hard to resist temptation.

People who are more extraverted are also more likely to cheat on their partner, the researchers found.

It is probably because extraverted people have a wider social circle and so more opportunities to cheat.

Also, extraverts are impulsive, sensation-seekers who can easily succumb to their desires.

The conclusions come from a survey of 208 people, who were asked about their relationships and whether they had cheated.

Up to 50% of people admit cheating on their partner, the authors write:

“Early studies reported that by the age of 40, 50% of all married men and more than 25% of all married women have engaged in extramarital sexual behavior.

Three decades later, an estimated 50% of men continued to engage in sexual and/or emotional extramarital relations while 40% of women engaged in similar relationships.”

The results of the study revealed that cheaters tend to be low in conscientiousness, extraverted and open to experience.

Extraverts tend to seek out stimulation, the authors write:

“Extroverts may be inclined to cheat to obtain stimulation and prevent boredom.

Extroversion may also facilitate less investment in the relationship when those with this trait seek out others for stimulation, thereby decreasing commitment and resulting in cheating behaviours.”

The third personality trait associated with infidelity is openness to experience.

Openness to experience is linked to intellect and creativity.

“…cheaters may perceive themselves as having stronger intellect and stronger creativity compared to that of their partners, leading them to seek out partners that may be a better, that is, similar, match.”

The study was published in the journal Current Psychology (Orzeck & Lung, 2005).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9594. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9593. Give Scrambled Eggs An Instant Flavor Boost With A Packet You Have In The Pantry

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you want an easy breakfast, eggs are key to a protein-rich morning meal that can be made in minutes — but for maximum flavor, you might want to think about scrambling them because you can mix them with any spice, herb, or seasoning you'd like. For example, pairing taco seasoning with your scrambled eggs creates an incomparable taste that requires only a few seconds of extra work.

For the simplest preparation, you can just whisk a teaspoon of the seasoning — we like McCormick Original Taco Seasoning Mix, available on Amazon — to about six eggs before you cook them, which will feed two to three people for breakfast. Most premade taco seasoning mixes contain plenty of salt, plus cumin, garlic powder, onion powder, and other spices, so you may be ready to go right out of the packet without needing to add anything else. But you can customize it to get exactly the flavor profile you're looking for.

If you're eating the eggs right off the plate, think about adding some cheese — Monterey Jack melts beautifully, and you can add a little extra spice with pepper jack. But cheddar is always a good choice and can add a sharper flavor, depending on what you use. For more creaminess, try Havarti, or go for Comté for some nutty undertones. From there, some freshly chopped cilantro or a drizzle of hot sauce makes for delicious toppings.

If you want to make a whole meal, you can add some extra ingredients to your plate. Putting a little chorizo in your scrambled eggs will give them a richer, spicier flavor, plus more protein. Or think about making summery breakfast tacos or burritos. You can cook sauteed onions, potatoes, and bell peppers, then mix it all together with your spiced eggs. All you need to do is wrap the mixture in your favorite tortilla, and you can enjoy it at the breakfast table or on the go.

#9591. 2 Supplements That Significantly Reduce Heart Disease And Cancer Risk

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil can significantly reduce heart attacks and vitamin D supplementation can significantly lower the number of deaths caused by different types of cancer.

Researchers studied 26,000 American adults in the VITAL clinical trial for five years to see if fish oil or vitamin D would definitely ward off cardiovascular disease or cancer.

The outcomes were reassuring: marine omega-3 fatty acid intake was linked to a significant drop in heart attacks.

One-and-half servings per week of dietary fish intake showed the maximum heart health benefits, but higher dietary fish intake didn’t help more.

The greatest decrease in heart attacks was seen in African-Americans.

The benefit of 1 gram of omega-3 fish oil supplementation showed a small decrease in major cardiovascular events like stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

Vitamin D3 or cholecalciferol intake at a dose of 2000 IU per day showed a significant decrease of death from cancer for those who took it for at least two years.

However, supplementation with vitamin D3 capsules didn’t significantly lower incidence of any type of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Dr. JoAnn Manson, the study’s first author, said:

“The pattern of findings suggests a complex balance of benefits and risks for each intervention and points to the need for additional research to determine which individuals may be most likely to derive a net benefit from these supplements.”

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, NAMS medical director, said:

“With heart disease and cancer representing the most significant health threats to women, it is imperative that we continue to study the viability of options that prevent these diseases and help women survive them.”

The 1 gram omega-3 fish oil supplementation used in the VITAL clinical trial was Omacor, a prescription medicine for adults.

The capsule contains 840 milligrams marine omega-3 fatty acids, of which 465 mg is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 375 mg is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

The study was presented at the North American Menopause Society (NAMS) Annual Meeting in Chicago (Manson et al., 2019).

#9590. No Beer, No Problem: Add A Splash Of This Drink For The Crunchiest Onion Rings

A top-tier onion ring brings together several textural qualities into one bite. You want enough heft to encase the slivers of allium, yet a crunchy consistency that's delicate. Each bite should contain both onion and batter, and while seasoning should be present, the onion's internal sweetness should still come through. It's a complex balance to get right, with beer often used as a cornerstone of the batter.

The beverage lends several advantages to onion rings: The hops and malt add flavor, the alcohol evaporates quickly during frying, and — most importantly — the carbonation creates an airy batter that translates to crunchiness. However, if you're not keen on adding a brew to your onion ring recipe, no fear: Sparkling water is a terrific alternative. Just like beer, the carbonation works its textural magic. And when used alongside rice flour (a tempura influence), you'll produce some of the crispiest onion rings, with an even more delicate texture.

It's critical to pour the sparkling water in as cold as possible — temperature control is essential for optimal crispness. As a result, you'll want to incorporate the water right out of the fridge, at the conclusion of batter preparation. Stir until the batter is homogeneous and on the liquidy side, similar to pancake or waffle batter in consistency. And you can also dredge the onions in flour separately first to make sure the breading sticks. Put the two elements together, deep-fry, and you'll get an onion ring rendition that is no less successful than a beer-based one.

Unlike beer and other flavored carbonated beverages, sparkling water's neutral flavor can be used to your advantage. Such a batter comes out lighter and without much added flavor, letting you tweak the seasonings to your liking. A rendition can be kept to a straightforward salt-only seasoning, which really puts the onions front and center. Or you can go with more flavorful spices like onion and garlic powder, paprika, and a dash of cayenne for heat. Don't rule out using some dried herbs in the batter, either; parsley flakes lend a nice herbal touch, for example. Apply seasoning both to the batter and after cooking to ensure comprehensive flavoring.

Want to up the crisp even further? Reach for some starchy ingredients other than flour and cornstarch. Dry potato flakes will lend your onion rings a pleasant starchy spin, and for an extra-golden-brown character, coat the dish with panko. Without beer in the mix, you can still achieve a light, airy texture. Serve them alongside homemade ranch, and it's an onion ring composition you'll want to make again and again.

#9587. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9586. Chris Ofili brings story of Laure—the Black model painted by Manet—in from the margins at Turin exhibition

Photo: Jack Hems. © Chris Ofili. Courtesy the artist and Victoria Miro

The UK artist Chris Ofili is rewriting the canon in a new show launching in Italy, giving one of Édouard Manet’s most famous figures—Laure, the Black model depicted in Manet’s Olympia (1863)—her own place in art history.

For the latest edition of Beyond the Collection curatorial initiative at the Pinacoteca Agnelli in Turin (30 October-4 April 2027), Ofili presents new works inspired by Laure including a large-scale painting, a watercolour and a series of drawings.

“[The exhibition] means questioning who has written our history and the exclusions involved,” said Sarah Cosulich, the director of the Pinacoteca Agnelli, at a press briefing. “Art historians rewrite history in their own way but Ofili brings this imaginative approach,” the exhibition curator Pietro Rigolo tells The Art Newspaper (Rigolo is also chief curator and head of collection at Pinacoteca Agnelli).

Among the works on view is Manet’s Portrait of Laure (La Négresse), around 1862, which is drawn from the Pinacoteca Agnelli's collection and has been renamed (the piece was originally entitled La Négresse).

Left: Édouard Manet's Portrait of Laure (La Négresse) (1862); Right: Chris Ofili

Images courtesy Pinacoteca Agnelli; Ofili portrait by Carlos Arias

“Ofili starts with this idea of giving back to this woman her name and her identity, giving her a story and presence,” Rigolo says. “Nobody has objected to the name change [of the work],” he adds.

Ofili’s large-scale painting, Saint Laure (2026), is the same size as Manet’s Olympia, in which Laure brings flowers to a nude, reclining Parisian courtesan. In his piece, Ofili turns Olympia’s body into a desert landscape which runs along the base of the work, shifting “Laure from the margins to the centre”, an exhibition statement says.

For the work, “Ofili looks to Italian and religious art—in particular depictions of angelic figures and artists such as Giotto and Fra Angelico (Beato Angelico)—and he also looked to an Italian movie called Io Capitano [2023],” Rigolo adds. Io Capitano follows two young Senegalese cousins on their journey from West Africa to Italy. “There is a debate in Italy about migration—this [Ofili] project is grounded in what is happening in Italy now,” Rigolo says, referencing the ongoing political issue polarising European countries. Ofili bases his depiction of Laure in particular on the film’s unnamed character known as “woman in the desert”.

Ofili’s new works also draw on the research of Denise Murrell, a curator-at-large at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Murrell has reshaped the role of the Black female figure in Modern art in her studies, as in the exhibition Posing Modernity: The Black Model from Manet and Matisse to Today, which opened at Columbia’s Wallach Art Gallery in 2018. “From the outset, Ofili said he wanted to involve Murrell [who contributes to a scholarly booklet accompanying the show],” Rigolo says.

The new season of exhibitions at the Pinacoteca Agnelli also include a retrospective dedicated to the 20th-century Greek-Italian painter and polymath Alberto Savinio, the brother of Giorgio de Chirico who played a fundamental role in the development of Metaphysical art (30 October-4 April 2027).

Next year, Ofili’s largest solo exhibition in London since his Tate Britain show in 2010 will open at the Hayward Gallery (7 September-9 January 2028). It will survey three decades of his practice and feature key works from the 1990s alongside his latest paintings.

Pinacoteca Agnelli art complex, housed in former Fiat factory, launches with Sylvie Fleury show and Picasso display

The event may be focused around Artissima, Italy’s leading art fair, but there's must-see exhibitions to found across the city

Exhibition at the Wallach Art Gallery includes works by Manet, Matisse and Mickalene Thomas

#9585. Add Cowboy Candy To Your Next Grilled Cheese For Triple The Flavor

Making the best grilled cheese can be serious business. And though the modern grilled cheese didn't take off until the 1920s — when commercially sliced bread and process cheese made it an affordable household staple — one perfect add-on for your next sandwich carries a classic frontier spirit. It's called cowboy candy — sugared and pickled jalapeño peppers — and each slice adds an incredible amount of flavor to your meal.

If you like the sweet and sour mix of bread and butter pickles, and you can handle a decent hit of spiciness, you'll love cowboy candy. When jalapeños are pickled, the brine can mellow their heat, so you won't just get a blast of intense spiciness. You'll get crunchy, vegetal, and herbaceous notes; some nice tang from the vinegar; plus a hit of sweetness. And it goes with just about any cheese you want to put on your sando. Cheddar or Monterey Jack are classic American options. If you want more nuttiness, you can try Gruyère, or give Havarti a go for some nice buttery flavor that would also be delicious with caramelized onions. And adding some spicy chorizo will make it a full meal.

The history of cowboy candy begins in the Lone Star State. WHH Ranch, which is based in Texas, claims to be the originator of the condiment and the oldest family-owned cannery in the state. These days, you can order a variety of cowboy candy versions from its website.

If you want to make cowboy candy at home, it's not hard to do on your own. You're going to need a mix of sugar, vinegar, and pickling spices. The mixture will cook down into a thick syrup to give the peppers a nice sugary coating that turns a regular spicy grilled cheese into a masterful mix of flavors. For the spices, you can go the standard route with mustard seeds, celery seeds, and turmeric for the tasty bread and butter pickle style. But a little dried or fresh dill will get you closer to a classic dill pickle flavor, and some chipotle pepper powder will add more smokiness. If you want more of a pungent tang, you can add some apple cider vinegar.

When you're making your cowboy candy grilled cheese, think about what cheeses will blend best with the sweet, spicy, savory flavor. Maybe try a nice sourdough or thick Texas toast, and don't be afraid to try some other protein additions. Turn it into a taco-inspired sandwich with some seasoned ground beef, or use up the leftovers from your rotisserie chicken. Just get that cowboy candy for your next grilled cheese, and from there, you can pile on the flavor.

#9582. 10 Best Chain Italian Subs, According To Customer Reviews

The Italian sub is its own category of cuisine. Born of the ingenuity of Italian immigrants, this centuries-old sandwich balances the highest forms of culinary technique with the simplest combination of ingredients. Expertly cured meats, creamy provolone cheese, crisp vegetables, and the right formula of oil and vinegar — all layered on a crusty roll, hoagie, or baguette — meld into a perfectly harmonious bite that's simultaneously salty, tangy, punchy, and fresh. Within this basic framework is room for limitless personalization. Some shops adorn their Italian sandwich with mayonnaise or hot relish. Another might add prosciutto or smoked ham or a stack of vinegary banana peppers. One may even toast the thing.

That's why the Italian sub is such a fun food to explore. No two are identical — even if they use exactly the same ingredients. Obviously, a sandwich with so much history is an easy target for dissection and judgment. Customers have their favorites, especially when it comes to what's offered at popular chain restaurants. And they're not afraid to share their feelings. For this article, I looked through hundreds of reviews, comments, and posts to find the Italian sub sandwiches with the highest customer ratings and feedback. The chains on this list range from dedicated sandwich spots to supermarkets to gas–station chains, but they all put together a great Italian sub.

With higher-quality ingredients, sliced-to-order meats, and lettuce shredded so thin it defies Newtonian mechanics, you could argue Jersey Mike's has successfully redefined the fast-casual sub. But a sandwich shop — especially one with the word "Jersey" in its name — is really only as good as its Italian sub. And in this department, Mike's Original Italian (AKA "The #13") delivers. It's a classic "Jersey-style" Italian sandwich, filled with provolone, ham, prosciuttini, capicola, salami, and pepperoni, creating a symphony of sweet, spicy, and savory meats.

"I went to Jersey Mike's for the first time and had one of the best subs I've had in a long time – #13 Italian sub done Mike's way," starts one Reddit thread. "13, Mike's way, add relish is the best Italian sandwich I have had since buying them from Italian bakeries as a kid." noted another commenter. The overall consensus is that Jersey Mike's takes pride in its product, and that getting the sandwich "Mike's Way," with a topping of tomato, onion, olive oil, red wine vinegar, oregano, and salt, elevates the experience to what you may find at a local Italian deli. It seems the community has spoken: Jersey Mike's is the best.

With over 2,500 locations across the country, Jimmy John's is one of the largest sandwich chains in the U.S., and while not all its sandwiches receive universal praise, one exception stands out: the JJ's Italian Night Club. And just like its major competitor, Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's doesn't reinvent the wheel with its Italian sandwich. It's a classic combination of meat (salami, capicola, ham), provolone cheese, onion, lettuce, tomato, mayo, oil, vinegar, and seasonings, all served on freshly baked French bread.

Customers love the bread at Jimmy John's — just not its appearance. "Their bread looks plain AF, but it really do hit," said one Redditor. "That bread looks sad, but the Italian night club with hot peppers is the only sandwich that gets my money there," mentioned another. To deal with this boring bread, regulars recommend toasting it to achieve a light-brown crust and accentuate its yeasty aroma. The aforementioned hot peppers are another game changer, adding a tart, vinegary bite and lingering heat that cuts through the otherwise rich and meaty sandwich. One insider suggests that, when ordering the hot peppers, ask for extra.

While Jersey Mike's and Jimmy John's have thousands of locations scattered throughout the country, there are a handful of smaller regional chains serving quality, thoughtfully assembled sub sandwiches. Penn Station is one of them. With over 300 restaurants across the South and Midwest, Penn Station is winning over the hearts (and stomachs) of its customers with a concentrated menu of subs, wraps, hand-crafted sandwiches, and seasonal specials. As with most sub chains, its Classic Grilled Italian is getting the most attention. Along with the typical ingredient lineup, Penn Station uses smoked ham and banana peppers, minor tweaks that add a little electricity to its signature sandwich.

On Reddit, the sandwich receives gushing adoration from regular customers. "Penn Station's Italian sub has a hold on me," starts one thread. A lot of the love has to do with the mayonnaise, which one person described as "otherworldly." But what makes up the bulk of every sub sandwich is its bread, and here, again, Penn Station doesn't falter, with several customers noting its flavor and texture as a main contributor to the chain's overall success.

DiBella's began as a neighborhood grocery store in upstate New York around a hundred years ago. A lot has changed in the centuries since, just not the quality of its sandwiches, which have remained undeniably delicious for decades. Now, I know that we've talked a lot about bread already, but DiBella's might produce the best loaf of the bunch. The dough is aged for a minimum of 16 hours, scored by hand, and baked fresh two times a day to ensure customers never bite into something even remotely stale, which is why one enthusiastic customer called it the GOAT.

Online, people are impressed that the chain can execute mom-and-pop level taste and freshness (and an impeccable meatball sub). "DiBella's is amazing...It's hard to believe it's a chain," noted a fan. But how's the sandwich itself? Well, with a name like DiBella's, you know that its signature sandwich, aptly named "The Godfather" delivers everything you could want in a good Italian sub. All in all, it's a very solid sandwich that needs to be on your radar.

Cheba Hut's branding reads like something from a college dorm room, but its food quality is anything but juvenile or half-baked. Across the board, Cheba Hut does solid sandwiches, but its La Canna has emerged as a fan favorite, with one thread titled "My New Favorite Sub," getting over 100 upvotes on Reddit.

The La Canna distinguishes itself from other Italian subs by using prosciutto in place of the more common capicola, along with Genoa salami and smoked ham. Equally important is the ingredient balance, which pairs crisp vegetables, meat, and cheese with a tangy "shake & house" dressing. "Can't beat a La Canna on garlic herb," said one Redditor. But what makes Cheba Hut so special is its general culture of sandwich lawlessness. There are few rules here; you can get your sandwiches with alfalfa sprouts or cream cheese, on garlic bread, or served alongside a bowl of French onion soup for dipping.

Potbelly doesn't get the respect it deserves. While most of the chains on this list specialize in sandwiches, Potbelly does it all: wraps, salads, soups, subs, chili, milkshakes, mac and cheese, and one of the best club sandwiches around. But with so much variety, it's easy to be fooled into thinking it's a "jack of all trades, master of none" scenario, but this isn't the case at all.

But the Italian sandwich, although slightly more conservative than its other sandwich offering, is still tasty and reliable. Unlike other chains, Potbelly offers four — not three — heavy-hitting meats, including salami, old-world capicola, pepperoni, and mortadella — a detail that only the most observant sandwich snobs appreciate. "Their Italian is the best chain sub shop Italian out there. Nowhere else has mortadella," noted a Redditor. Others appreciate the sandwich, as well, with one person saying it's their "top choice for a commercial chain place." But what really sets this sandwich apart from the others is the giardiniera, a quintessential Chicago topping of hot pickled peppers, carrots, celery, and other veggies. The condiment is so desirable that Potbelly even sells it by the jar.

Unlike some of the other sandwich chains on this list, PrimoHoagies specializes in Italian subs. And that distinction, especially for a Philadelphia-based operation, leaves little room for error. PrimoHoagies is so committed to the Italian sandwich that it offers not one, not two, but five different variations, each with a different formula of sweet, spicy, and sharp meats and cheeses. Online, the sandwiches at PrimoHoagie's are both widely celebrated and the source of debate, specifically for the quantity of meat packed between its bread.

But many customers think this is a good problem and actually appreciate the quantity and value. In many ways, this is the most authentic sandwich of the bunch. It doesn't come with bells and whistles, just a short list of quality ingredients layered on an "award-winning seeded bread." And if you really have an issue with the quantity of cold cuts, just ask the sandwich makers for some extra veggies.

No one thinks twice about grabbing groceries at a supermarket, but for whatever reason, when it comes to prepared foods — especially sandwiches — shoppers are a little more hesitant. But when you really think about it, the supermarket, with its endless inventory of fresh vegetables, breads, meats, and cheeses, is the ideal place to grab a sub. Publix, a chain of grocery stores popular in Florida and the Southern United States, has made a name for itself in the sandwich department. Whereas other supermarkets haphazardly throw their sandwiches together, Publix constructs its subs with care and attention.

Online, customers voice their appreciation. "There are few things better in life than a Pub Sub," mentioned a Redditor. And despite being a regional supermarket chain, Publix has legions of followers across the country who will make a special trip whenever they're nearby. The supermarket's Italian sub, which comes with the classic trio of meats and provolone, isn't revolutionary, but what sets the sandwich apart is the quality of the vegetables and freshly-baked Italian Five Grain sub roll. Add some oil and vinegar for a perfectly balanced bite.

Wawa has a cult following, and for good reason. Its to-go meals, subs, sides, and secret off-menu items are terrific, even compared to fast-casual chains dedicated specifically to the craft of sandwich making. If you're unfamiliar with Wawa, you can order via a handy touchpad, where you can order sandwiches as-is or customize them to your preferences. If you suffer from choice paralysis, its predesigned subs are a terrific option. One that constantly scores high marks is its Italian sub.

In a ranking of all the Wawa subs (or hoagies if you're from Philadelphia), The Takeout declared the Italian the best option, citing its flavorful collection of meats and deft blend of salty, spicy, and fresh ingredients. This is far from a fluke. One Reddit thread dedicated to Wawa's Italian Sub has over 400 upvotes, with users describing their specific orders in the comments. Some people go standard, but many regulars like to add extra meat and cheese, jalapeños, oil and vinegar, or garlic aioli. But it's the entire Wawa experience that has won over the hearts of its customers. You can fill up your gas tank, grab a quick sandwich, and be back on the road in just a few minutes.

Another gas station moonlighting as a fast-casual stop for quality grub, QuickChek isn't so different from Wawa. And the same goes for the quality of its subs. Both chains offer a similar digital ordering platform where customers can choose every aspect of their sandwich, from the toppings to the bread. Sub sandwiches shouldn't leave you hungry, and QuickChek is a bang for your buck. But don't take our word for it. In 2021, QuickChek was named the "Best Value" for Italian subs in New Jersey, according to New Jersey Monthly.

And when you see some of its sandwiches, you'll know why. One of its Signature Subs, the Giant Italian, lives up to its name: a mammoth foot-long sub loaded with ham, salami, pepperoni, fresh mozzarella, tomato, onion, lettuce, garlic aioli, and a dynamite cherry pepper relish. On Facebook, regulars agree that for the price, speed, and accessibility, it's hard to beat a QuickChek sandwich. It's all love for this affordable convenience chain.

#9579. Make Your Scrambled Eggs Cracker Barrel-Style With This Easy Method (No Butter Required)

Cracker Barrel's best-selling menu item is a classic pancake, bacon, and egg combo, and no small part of that is because of the eggs. But according to a self-identified employee on Reddit, the old-timey establishment achieves such a delicious breakfast by keeping things simple, cooking them on a griddle with just canola oil — no butter.

When you include abundant fat in scrambled eggs, they slow down the coagulation of protein curds and keep them creamy and rich. By opting for a quick spray of canola oil instead, you can achieve a wildly different texture, allowing those proteins to join together for something a bit more solid and with a slight chew. Griddles also allow maximum surface area contact with direct heat, helping them cook quickly without burning them or making them tough. This is partially why breaking out the griddle is great when making breakfast for a crowd, and you can always add other foods like pancakes and bacon while you prepare the eggs.

Since you won't be able to rely on fat for texture, it's also important to use Cracker Barrel's preferred griddle temperature of 225 degrees Fahrenheit. This is closer to a medium heat, which keeps the eggs fluffy but still not quite creamy. The restaurant also employs one expert tip for quality scrambled eggs: using farm-fresh ingredients. These have a richer flavor to compensate for less fat and firmer whites to help keep the fluffy shape while you eat them.

When a breakfast item is so good but also so simple, a lot of its quality boils down to technique. Cooking with less fat gives you a smaller margin of error, and a griddle can take some getting used to, so keep your eggs in constant motion and don't be afraid to lean on a bit of added water to level up your breakfast.

When you cook scrambled eggs in a small pan, even a small amount will quickly drop its temperature. The same isn't necessarily true for a griddle, especially if you use one with a heavy-duty steel cooktop that retains a ton of heat, but it also responds quickly when the flame is lowered, allowing precise control of temperature throughout cooking. Using two spatulas to continuously move and fold your eggs is a great way to help them cook evenly. Plus, the successive folded layers only build on all that fluffiness and make them fantastic as an ingredient in things like a breakfast sandwich or burrito.

When it comes to keeping eggs fluffy, but not too rich or runny, your best bet is a simple splash of water. Added moisture, but no fat, steams the curds a bit, helping them plump up without growing dense. While too much will make them soupy and flavorless, a tablespoon per three eggs does a great job. The added moisture also helps prevent them from drying out when using something as hot and fast as a large surface area griddle, so it can be a great tool if you've never cooked on a flat-top before.

#9578. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9576. The Canadian Bacon In A McDonald's Egg McMuffin Isn't Slow-Brined

Along with the fact that the McDonald's Egg McMuffin is endlessly customizable (even the simple addition of extra butter upgrades the sandwich), its base ingredients make for a bite that is a symphony of rich, savory flavors and includes enough variety of textures to keep your mouth interested until the very end. One of the most compelling components of the once good, now great McMuffin is the Canadian bacon: the thin, disc-shaped meat that seemingly has more in common with ham than the crispy strips we associate with bacon. It might interest you to know that this tender slab of pork doesn't get its salty flavor from a slow brine, or really, any immersive procedure at all. Instead, the brine is actually injected into the meat during the manufacturing process, according to Food Tech Today (per YouTube).

McDonald's hasn't publicly released which of its partners actually produces its Canadian bacon, but it's as good a guess as any that it could be Lopez Foods, a long-time known beef supplier for the burger chain. Whoever manufactures the Canadian bacon, though, does so by following a highly mechanized process, where the pork loins, fresh from the slaughterhouse, go through a series of machines in the plant. One of these machines contains hundreds of needles that automatically inject the brine, made mostly of salt, sugar, sodium nitrate, and food coloring, into the trimmed but still largely unprocessed pork as it travels down the production line. The brine is necessary for flavor, as well as texture, to ensure the meat stays tender and juicy.

The journey those pork loins make from the moment they enter the processing plant until they end up as slices on a McDonald's McMuffin is actually fascinating, and no part is more interesting than the second half of the operation. This is where the pork is packed tightly into sleeves, steamed for around five hours until fully cooked, and the brine has the opportunity to permeate and distribute all throughout the meat. Then, the tubes of pork are sliced into exact discs by a machine and placed in its vacuum-sealed packaging. Instead of arriving frozen at McDonald's locations, as the sausage does, the Canadian bacon arrives merely refrigerated.

To cook the Canadian bacon and give it the requisite browning that appears on the finished McMuffin, employees simply grab a number of the slices and place them down in the front of the clamshell grills, so that they're not under the lid. They cook for eight seconds on each side, and unlike McDonald's burgers, which don't get flipped, an employee must manually turn them over. The precise timing allows the slices to warm through, but not cook for so long that they crisp up, which could then be a hop, skip, and a jump away from burning and wasting Canadian bacon.

#9574. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9573. Former McDonald's Chef Reveals Why Fast Food Chicken Tenders Are Smaller Than They Look

From accusations of serving heavily processed food to concerns about the temperature of scalding coffee, fast food chains have faced their fair share of backlash over the years. One thing they could usually fall back on was offering an affordable meal, but with soaring prices, that promise is becoming harder to keep. And while customers have certainly felt the rising costs, they've not noticed a corresponding increase in quality. In fact, some are beginning to question whether they're really getting any bang for their buck at all.

Enter shrinkflation, the increasingly common practice of charging more while quietly reducing portion sizes. Even more frustratingly, some chains might be selling you a product that looks perfectly generous on the outside but contains surprisingly little actual meat. In a documentary produced by More Perfect Union, former McDonald's corporate chef Mike Haracz revealed some industry tricks fast food chains use to make their chicken tenders look bigger than they actually are. Right off the bat, Haracz explained why some chains compromise on product quality in the first place. "They are willing to serve not as good of a product because they can make more money and serve more people," he shared. "Make it as cheap as possible, so they can get the most profit."

So how exactly do they pull it off? According to Haracz, there's more than one way to make a chicken tender like bigger without actually adding more chicken. One approach involves the marinade. By injecting or soaking the meat in a saltwater brine, manufacturers can increase its moisture content and weight, making the tender appear plumper. Then there's the breading. Using a thicker coating, double-dredging the chicken, or opting for bulkier panko breadcrumbs can all add extra volume to the finished product.

It's no secret that nobody likes shrinkflation. Just look at the brutal way those accused of it were treated in the Middle Ages. These days, however, mob justice has largely been replaced by people venting their frustrations on Reddit. Reacting to the More Perfect Union video, one Redditor wrote, "Any company that is publicly traded has a fiduciary duty to sell you the worst possible product for the most money possible. Fast food is no exception." This user might be onto something since chicken tenders aren't the only fast food product that has been accused of shrinkflation.

According to Fox News, chicken is the number one best-selling fast food protein on DoorDash, with beef burgers not far behind. While anything labeled 100% ground beef legally cannot contain added water, and coating it in extra breading is obviously out of the question, that doesn't mean chains are short on other tricks to cut costs and make their beef go further. According to the More Perfect Union documentary, one common approach is to use beef with a lower lean-to-fat ratio, which is typically cheaper than leaner blends. However, the price trade-off becomes apparent once the patty hits the grill.

As the fat renders out during cooking, the burger can shrink considerably, leaving you with a smaller finished patty than you might expect from its raw weight — and it's the raw weight that most fast food joints use in advertising. Another trick involves the toppings themselves. By reducing the size of ingredients like lettuce, tomatoes, pickles, and even the bun, restaurants can make them more proportionate to a smaller patty, helping maintain the illusion of a generously filled burger even when there's less meat underneath.

#9571. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).
